title: Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism
content_c:
Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism
- Published
The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky ahead of this afternoon's talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country.
Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!"
But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner?
The two men have never been close – that much is obvious – but have they now fallen out once and for all?
Both in rhetoric and actions, the past ten days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship.
Just listen to the way they talk about each other.
"Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week.
The verbal assault has continued this week.
"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history.
Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously.
In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, saying Benjamin Netanyahu "has no f**king judgement". Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister".
"Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad."
For his part Zelensky has generally been circumspect in how he describes his unreliable but vital American counterpart.
But this month his frustration has been clear. Addressing a US congressional delegation, he spoke of "decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends" and voiced the fear that "some political decision has been made to slow down support for us."
Answering Trump's charge that he represented the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement, Zelensky sounded more exasperated than ever.
"We have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war with dignity," he wrote on Telegram on Monday.
But rhetoric aside, how bad is the relationship?
In some ways, we've been here before.
After their notorious televised bust up in the Oval Office in February 2025, at which Trump accused Zelensky of "gambling with World War III", the US suspended military assistance and restricted intelligence sharing.
The crisis only lasted a week. And when the Trump administration decided, later that year, that it no longer wanted to finance direct military assistance to Ukraine, a mechanism was put in place for European countries to pay for American equipment instead.
One exception, in the wake of this year's US war with Iran, has been badly needed US-made Patriot air defence missiles.
Amid a global shortage, the supply to Ukraine has slowed to a trickle, making it harder than ever for Kyiv to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.
The Washington Post, quoting an unnamed Ukrainian official, said "only a couple" of Patriot interceptors remained in Ukraine's stockpile, and that the Trump administration had slowed down the process by which US allies seek approval to transfer their stocks.
Similar concerns have been voiced in the past, but the latest reports – not confirmed by US officials – come against an increasingly difficult backdrop for Kyiv.
Earlier this month, as Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami for talks with Trump's all-purpose envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner, they were blindsided by the news that the president had just struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to open US markets to Russian diesel.
Experts questioned whether it would do much to drive down US petrol prices, ahead of congressional mid-term elections (the apparent motive), but as a signal of US displeasure over Ukraine's campaign of long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and Washington's willingness to do deals with the Kremlin, it represented a stinging rebuke to Kyiv.
Last Friday, Trump went further, waiving wide-ranging sanctions on Russia just two days before they were due to take effect.
Trump said the sanctions contained in the Graham Act (named after the former South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who died in July) would hinder his efforts to broker peace. But for Kyiv and its supporters this was another alarming sign that the White House was siding with the Kremlin.
"What the Trump administration is doing is providing carrots to the Russians and sticks to the Ukrainians," former US ambassador to Kyiv William Taylor told the BBC.
"It's inexplicable and saddening."
Kiriil Dmitriev, a senior Putin envoy, called it "an important and truly historic moment".
For Moscow, this felt like a welcome return to the "spirit of Alaska", a phrase much touted by Russian officials in the wake of the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage in August 2025.
Adding to the impression that Trump is turning his back on Ukraine is the allegation – again not confirmed by Washington – that the US has restricted the flow of intelligence and interfered with Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet service.
Amid an escalation in Russia's drone and missile war on Ukraine's cities, Kyiv says advance warning provided by US satellite intelligence has been lacking.
"We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky told NBC News.
On 12 October five Russian S-400 missiles hit Kyiv, reportedly before air raid sirens or mobile alerts had sounded.
The US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, denied there had been any pause in intelligence sharing, blaming a "software problem" for the temporary lack of early warnings.
Similar uncertainty surrounds Ukraine's access to Starlink.
A week ago, Ukrainian officials reported that the system was being throttled, with terminals unable to maintain connections at high speeds, making it harder for Ukraine's military to intercept fast moving Russian drones.
Since the summer, Ukraine has struggled to cope with a wave of attacks by advanced, jet-powered drones.
It's not clear where any order to limit Ukraine's use of Starlink – or its military grade equivalent Starshield – originated. Reuters reported that it came from the White House.
Rubio said "no-one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet."
But the fact that such suspicions surface so frequently points to the lack of trust that continues to infect US-Ukrainian relations.
Much of this has its roots in Donald Trump's seemingly long-standing mistrust of Ukraine as a whole - and Zelensky in particular.
A decade ago, Trump became convinced that Ukraine had tried to prevent him from becoming US president. Among a number of unfounded allegations was the suggestion that the US Democratic National Committee had a server hidden somewhere in Ukraine.
When Zelensky became president, three years later, he resisted Trump's demands that he investigate charges of election interference.
During a notorious July 2019 telephone conversation, Trump also asked Zelensky to investigate Joe Biden, the man who went on to defeat him in the 2020 presidential election. Again, Zelensky refused.
At the time, the White House was withholding $391m (£290m) in military assistance to Ukraine, a juxtaposition that ultimately led to Trump's first impeachment.
Whether Trump's resentment over these historic slights continues to inform his current policy towards Ukraine is an open question, but it's clear that the roller coaster of US-Ukraine relations has taken another stomach-churning dip.
Following the talks in Oslo, Witkoff is taking a set of updated proposals to St Petersburg. All eyes will now be on Putin.
Jonas Gahr Støre, the Norwegian leader, said the talks in Oslo had helped "to straighten out a few things."
"There's nothing to gain from… digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago," he said diplomatically.
Zelensky said the day had begun with a productive conversation with the US Secretary of State and indicated that the issue of early warning had already been fixed. He also sounded optimistic about Patriot missiles and Starlink.
"I think we will have good results too," he said.
Yet despite the optimistic tone, it's hard to get around the fact that Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump appear, once again, to be at loggerheads.
  - Published3 days ago

title: Government failings allowed Covid 'to spread like wildfire' in care homes, inquiry finds
content_c:
Government failings allowed Covid 'to spread like wildfire' in care homes, inquiry finds
- Published
Government failures in care settings created an environment that allowed Covid to spread like wildfire, an official inquiry has said.
The sixth report from the Covid inquiry said the care sector appeared to be "something of an afterthought" in the early stages of the pandemic and there was no "protective ring" put around homes as claimed by ministers at the time.
There were more than 43,000 recorded deaths involving Covid in care homes between March 2020 and July 2022.
The 287-page report also highlighted shortages of PPE for carers and criticised the way hospital patients were discharged into care homes.
It said limits on visits caused enormous harm to residents and their loved ones, though it blamed this on care homes themselves.
Around 1.5 million adults were either living in care homes or receiving support in their own homes when Covid hit.
Action to protect them came too late, causing devastating consequences, the inquiry said.
Chair Baroness Hallet said a lack of testing, PPE and pre-pandemic planning combined with policy decisions early on "created an environment in which the virus could spread like wildfire".
"At the critical early stages of the pandemic, not enough was done to protect those living and working in care homes," she said.
"The overriding focus of the UK government and devolved administrations was on protecting hospitals."
- Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says 
  - Published17 hours ago
- Covid inquiry PPE report - key findings 
  - Published14 July
Lack of PPE and financial support for carers
At the start of the pandemic, the then-Health Secretary Matt Hancock said the government had placed a protective ring around care homes.
But the report said that this claim was unfounded.
It also found:
- a lack of PPE meant staff had to resort to make-shift workarounds, including bins bags, festival waterproof ponchos and painters' overalls
- the decision to discharge hospitals patients into care homes at the start of the pandemic was understandable, but guidance should have made clear they needed to be isolated. This did not happen in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, which was a significant oversight
- a lack of financial support for care workers at the start of the pandemic made it difficult to allow them to stay away from their job if they were infected
- long-standing weakness in the care sector, including financial struggles and staff shortages, exacerbated problems
- by September 2020, evidence suggested care home visitors posed only a marginal infection risk, yet many care homes failed to ease restrictions in line with updated UK guidance, contributing to a significant decline in residents' health and wellbeing.
- there was evidence of blanket do-not-resuscitate orders being put in place in some care homes, which is considered unlawful
- millions of unpaid carers were left to take on evermore complex care and struggled because of a lack of support
Jean Adamson, of the Covid-19 Bereaved Families for Justice UK, said: "Today's report is a devastating account of one of the darkest episodes in our country's history.
"It shows that the government knew the care sector was extremely vulnerable to a pandemic and yet did nothing. Failing to act until it was too late."
Totally exposed
Caroline, Abrahams, the charity director at Age UK, said the report was "devastating".
"When Covid took off, people using social care and the staff and unpaid carers providing it were left totally exposed."
She added it also demonstrated how important the overhaul of social care promised by Andy Burnham when he became prime minister was.
"If a national care service had already been in place... the various disasters that befell social care during the pandemic would have been lessened and some might have been avoided altogether."
Meanwhile, Natalie Grayson, from the GMB union, said care workers were "left vulnerable and terribly exposed" during the pandemic which saw "care homes turned into morgues".
"That cannot be allowed to happen again," she added.
Nadra Ahmed, co-chair of the National Care Association, which represents care providers in England described the findings as "really upsetting", adding that the social care workforce has "never fully recovered" from the pandemic.
She said we need to "start thinking about social care in a more constructive way" and the mantra that "we all had to protect the NHS" appears to have come at the cost of "some care home residents' lives".
Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the government would provide a "full response" to the report's recommendations "in due course".
Speaking in the Commons, Cooper said she agreed that social care had been "undervalued and under-recognised" for too long.
"My thoughts are with all those who lost loved ones in the pandemic, and especially those who endured the immense distress and harm of visiting restrictions in care homes, which meant they could not be with loved ones even as they died," she added.

title: Union attacks NatWest plans to get workers back to the office
content_c:
Union attacks NatWest plans to get workers back to the office
- Published
The Unite union has hit out at a plan by NatWest to reduce the rights of 30,000 of its employees to work from home.
NatWest says it is moving to a hybrid approach where workers will be required to attend the office at least two days a week, from February.
The bank says this is still very competitive with the rest of the finance industry, and exceptions will be made for colleagues who require additional flexibility.
But Unite said NatWest's decision was "out of touch with the realities facing its workforce", with many facing higher travel and childcare costs.
Firms have been gradually drawing people back into the office since working from home became the norm for some office workers during the Covid pandemic.
In January last year, Amazon required staff to return to the office five days a week after they had been working two days at home.
Other firms such as Boots and JP Morgan have brought in policies requiring head office staff to be in every day.
But Barclays faced a backlash from staff last month over plans to require workers to go to the office three days a week. It brought in a longer transition period in response to staff and union complaints.
Unite said NatWest was abolishing its "remote first" employment category, which allows 13,497 workers to attend the office around twice a month, and requiring 17,272 hybrid workers to increase their office attendance.
The union says that many of the affected workers are lower-paid grades, and the new requirements will increase cost-of-living pressures, while disrupting the arrangements of disabled workers and carers.
In a statement, Unite general secretary Sharon Graham called NatWest's move a "kick in the teeth" for its workers.
"Thousands of workers face higher travel and childcare costs and disruption to caring responsibilities," she said
"For NatWest to impose these changes while reneging on existing agreements shows complete contempt for its workforce."
Graham called on NatWest to "ditch these proposals and engage properly with its workers".
A NatWest spokesman said: "Flexible working remains an important part of how we work but we've also learned more about the value that spending time together brings for our colleagues and customers - helping teams collaborate, share ideas, build relationships and learn from one another.
"That's why we're introducing a more consistent approach across the bank, with colleagues expected to spend at least two days a week in the office, depending on the needs of their role and business area.
"We recognise this will be a change for some colleagues and we're giving them time to plan ahead and will support them through the transition."

title: Flavio Bolsonaro’s ‘corrupto’ stunt sparks viral meme before Brazil election runoff
content_c:
To Flávio Bolsonaro and his publicists, it must have seemed an ingenious idea that would expose his rival’s supposed crookedness on the eve of Brazil’s presidential election.
But the far-right politician’s decision to attend a primetime television debate against his leftwing opponent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, with the word “corrupto” (corrupt) written on the palm of his hand has backfired.
Rather than drawing attention to the incumbent’s alleged misdeeds, many of the programme’s millions of viewers sarcastically took Bolsonaro’s hand-written message as an admission of his own guilt.
Following Sunday night’s debate, Lula supporters from all walks of life have flooded social media with photographs of their own self-descriptions inked on their palms.
John Ulhoa, the guitarist from a pop rock band called Pato Fu, jokingly described himself as a “musician (and a hunk)”.
The Emmy-winning comedian Antonio Tabet introduced himself to his 2.8 million followers on X as an artist.
Carlos Marcio used both palms to portray himself as a cellist and author.
Carla Emanuela Sacramento, an obstetric nurse, posted a photograph of herself clad in personal protective equipment and with the words “primary health care nurse” proudly written on her right palm.
Prominent politicians also jumped on the trend, including Lula’s health minister, the infectious disease specialist Alexandre Padilha, whose palm noted he was a doctor, and Tabata Amaral, who identified as a political scientist and astrophysicist.
All across the country, librarians, oil workers, engineers, journalists, architects, pilots, psychologists, seamstresses, street cleaners, teachers, influencers, and police officers used ballpoint pens to inscribe their professions on to their skin.
Writing on Substack, the Latin America expert James Bosworth called Bolsonaro’s stunt a “critical error” in his bid for power.
“It may have seemed like an inspired pre-debate gimmick. Instead, he gave the world a meme image that will stick with him for the rest of his political career,” Bosworth said, offering politicians a word of advice.
“Don’t write the word ‘corrupto’ on your hand and show it to the audience,” Bosworth suggested.
Bolsonaro, who is the son of the jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, is a professional politician who has long faced corruption accusations, although he denies them and has never been convicted. The 45-year-old senator also has well-documented ties to members of Rio’s mafia underworld and once employed the relatives of the city’s most notorious contract killer, Adriano da Nóbrega. Last week two allies were arrested for alleged involvement with the Red Command drug faction, which Donald Trump recently designated a foreign terrorist organisation. Bolsonaro voiced surprise at those arrests and said the men had the right to prove their innocence.
On Monday, Brazilian media reported that Bolsonaro was being investigated by the federal police as part of a money-laundering inquiry.
Lula, whose Worker’s party (PT) has also been involved in major corruption scandals, used Sunday’s debate to throw down the gauntlet to Bolsonaro.
The leftwing incumbent said he would give electoral authorities access to his banking and phone recordings, and those of close relatives, in order to prove he was not corrupt – if Bolsonaro agreed to do the same.
Bolsonaro, who, polls suggest, holds a slender advantage ahead of Sunday’s second-round runoff, has yet to respond to Lula’s challenge. The rightwinger won the 4 October first round by more than 2m votes.

title: From strife-torn France to the UK, rightwing populists win when they stir chaos while promising order  | Rafael Behr
content_c:
An election where one side represents chaos will nearly always be won by the party that promises order instead. Public fatigue after years of turbulent Tory rule accounted for Labour’s 2024 landslide victory more than any policy in Keir Starmer’s manifesto. Across the Channel, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally (RN), is currently on course to win next year’s presidential poll with a pledge of “restored authority and security” for a country that has spent years cycling between enervating stasis and explosive crisis.
Le Pen has been boosted in recent days by scenes of city centres ablaze and shops being looted as student demonstrations mutated into riots. Street confrontation is a more standard feature of the political repertoire in France than in most settled democracies, but the destruction was disturbing by any measure.
President Emmanuel Macron’s government, debilitated by the lack of a parliamentary majority, looked unprepared for the scale of the unrest. There was ample indication that something big was brewing. What began with high school students despairing at the neglected state of secondary education evolved into a general mobilisation of anger at high living costs and a lack of economic opportunities. Aggressive police tactics radicalised the crowd. As night followed day, and just as predictably, political fury gave way to opportunistic pillaging.
Prime minister Sébastien Lecornu accused “ultra-left” provocateurs of stirring disorder as part of a strategy to render the country ungovernable in the run-up to next year’s elections. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the populist left’s presidential candidate, countered that violence was the natural byproduct of a degenerate repressive state that conspires to discredit resistance, and that the protests channelled the heroic spirit of May 1968.
At 75, Mélenchon is old enough to remember that Paris spring of revolutionary fervour. He has a keen following in the current generation of activist students, but the insurrectionary rhetoric unsettles swathes of conservative France. His pungency could put Le Pen in the Élysée Palace.
In the past she has been locked out of the presidency by coalitions of moderate and left voters rallying, often without enthusiasm, behind the candidate best placed to stop her. RN’s advances in parliament have been checked in the same way, although it is currently the biggest party.
Macron has twice been the beneficiary of that dynamic, but he can’t run again, has no obvious successor and is so radioactively unpopular that the whole liberal centre ground is contaminated by his standing on it.
Current polling indicates that the “republican front” would unravel if the only names in a second-round run-off were Mélenchon and Le Pen. The centre-right would break for the RN leader. It probably wouldn’t even be close.
France’s crisis has not escaped notice across the Atlantic, where it is viewed through the warped lens of Maga ideology. Donald Trump explained that “France is burning” because the country has been overrun by immigrants “with hatred in their hearts”. JD Vance agreed that “western liberals” were to blame for opening European borders to “the third world” and advised American voters to view French misfortune as a premonition of the future if Congress is captured by Democrats in midterm elections next month.
Republican efforts to cast their rivals as catalysts of national ruin have limited traction when Trump is the obvious engine of chaos. Democrats didn’t start the war in Iran. Nor did they author a deranged trade policy that alienated the US’s friends, turning even Canada into a foe.
This is a common problem for incumbent demagogues. In opposition, simple solutions are proposed for complex problems: tariffs as the remedy for industrial decline; expelling illegal immigrants as the answer to every social and economic grievance; trusting in the leader’s judgment as the answer to everything else.
In office, those mechanisms fail to deliver the promised benefits. Someone needs to be blamed. The categories of undesirable element grow. Media, universities, courts and opposition parties are called crooked or treasonous. But purges disrupt the smooth running of a country. They are bad for the economy. This is how the insecure leader goes through the gears of tyranny. A craving for control generates dissent, which is attacked as a menace to society, requiring more draconian law enforcement. When that provokes more determined opposition, the dissenters are denounced as extremists who jeopardise public safety.
Trump has travelled some way down that road already. He might accelerate a lot further after the midterms. One option is to make bogus claims of election fraud, denying the validity of results that, if allowed to stand, would empower Democrats to hold a rogue president to account. His despotic temperament and his record of refusal to admit any electoral weakness suggest he would rather trigger a constitutional crisis of existential dimensions for American democracy than acquiesce to cohabitation with an unfriendly Congress. He will plunge the country deeper into chaos and insist that the nation rally around him as the only one capable of restoring order.
That is standard authoritarian operating procedure. The arsonists affect dismay at the conflagrations they ignite. They cavort in firefighter costumes and hose the flames with petrol.
This is the role Le Pen is readying herself for now in France. If she wins next year’s election, the backlash from the left will be ferocious. That challenge will be eagerly confronted by an incoming president likely to be looking for pretexts to declare a national emergency and remake the republic as a vehicle for her personal authority.
Britain’s radical right parties dream of an equivalent opportunity. They revel in lurid imagery of societal breakdown. Sometimes the fantasy is camouflaged as a warning about the dangers of unchecked immigration, but impatience for a violent reckoning is never far from the surface. For Rupert Lowe, leader of Restore Britain, there is seemingly no effort to conceal the relish. He told his followers on X last week that his agenda would certainly trigger “civil unrest and rioting,” and that “what needs to happen will be incredibly painful”.
Lowe is still a relatively fringe figure but he exerts disproportionate influence in the conservative digital ecosystem thanks to amplification on X by Elon Musk, the platform’s oligarch proprietor. Lowe’s candidate beat the Tories and Liberal Democrats in Manchester’s mayoral byelection earlier this year. By competing for votes with Reform UK, Restore Britain has drawn Nigel Farage into an arms race in fanatical anti-migrant rhetoric.
Farage’s status as a more serious contender in the electoral arena allows him to launder ideas that were once self-evidently extreme – mass deportations, for example – as mainstream policy. That doesn’t automatically make them popular. There is an audience for ethnically selective nationalism but it has a ceiling. The voters who are motivated by determination to thwart Farage outnumber those who want him installed in Downing Street.
That tactical coalition is easily galvanised because prominent figures on the British right wear their arsonist intent so brazenly. Also, a stable Labour government isn’t giving them opportunities to play at being firefighters.
To advance on power, Reform UK has to win over the kinds of voters that Le Pen sees heading her way through the smouldering rubble of French politics: people exhausted and bewildered by the system unravelling, without hope that incumbent authorities can get the country back on track, and amenable to the argument that fanatical leftists are the more menacing agents of chaos. Thankfully, those are not the conditions of British politics. Andy Burnham’s every step should be guided by the need to keep it that way.
- 
  Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

title: Portugal housing protests continue after police clear camps
content_c:
Portugal housing protests continue after police clear camps
October 21, 2026
Thousands of people rallied in Lisbon, Porto and other Portuguese cities on Tuesday evening, hours after police dismantled protest camps and arrested a total of 55 demonstrators.
The protesters vowed to continue their campaign against Portugal's deepening housing crisis, which has made buying or renting a home increasingly unaffordable.
Organizers said more than 1,000 people gathered in each of the two main protest locations, although police did not provide crowd estimates. 
In Lisbon's central Rossio square, demonstrators voted by a show of hands to re-establish their tent camp on Wednesday.
Police moves to shut down protest camps
Police launched coordinated operations in Lisbon and Porto shortly before 6 a.m. (0500 GMT) on Tuesday, after warning protesters that their camps were illegal.
Activists had occupied Lisbon's Rossio square since Saturday, setting up around 200 tents. In Porto, protesters had camped in Dom Joao I square for about 10 days.
Authorities seized 228 camping structures during the operation.
In Porto, demonstrators dismantled their tents themselves after police threatened to intervene. In Lisbon, officers cleared the square as protesters formed a human chain.
Clashes subsequently broke out, according to footage broadcast by local television stations.
Carla Valadao, a spokesperson for the Lisbon camp, described the operation as "very aggressive."
However, Public Security Police superintendent Sergio Soares disputed that account, saying the eviction had been "calm, proportionate and appropriate, with no police charge."
All 55 people arrested were later released pending a court appearance in Lisbon on Wednesday.
Why are people protesting in Portugal?
Portugal is struggling with one of Europe's worst housing affordability crises.
Property purchase prices have more than doubled since 2017, while rents for new leases have nearly doubled over the same period.
The problem is particularly severe in major cities such as Lisbon and Porto, where residents have also protested against excessive tourism and an influx of so-called digital nomads.
Demonstrators accuse the center-right government of failing to address the crisis.
They are demanding the withdrawal of a bill that would make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases. The proposed legislation has already passed its first parliamentary reading.
Debora Miranda, a 41-year-old communications consultant, told Reuters she joined the Lisbon demonstration to represent generations struggling with rising housing costs.
"If people don't feel at home, in every sense of the word, they can't move forward with their lives...enough is enough."
Jorge Paixao, a 19-year-old history student, described the situation as "a societal crisis."
He said his generation needed "the ability to live with dignity, start families and rejuvenate Portugal."
Portugal housing protest takes place amid demos around Europe
The demonstrations come amid growing anger over housing affordability and living costs across several European countries.
Protesters in Portugal have sought to align their movement with similar demonstrations in neighboring Spain.
In Madrid, activists maintain a tent camp to call for stronger action to tackle the housing crisis. The crisis was sparked by the eviction ofMaria del Carmen Abascal from her home.
The nearly four weeks of protests in Spain have contributed to political turmoil, leading to a snap general election being called for November 29.
Meanwhile, demonstrations over rising living costs have also taken place in France, Belgium and Italy.
Violence that erupted in France over the weekend on the sidelines of otherwise peaceful protests has raised concerns that similar unrest could spread to other countries facing comparable economic pressures.
Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

In Madrid, activists maintain a tent camp to call for stronger action to tackle the housing crisis. The crisis was sparked by the eviction ofMaria del Carmen Abascal from her home.
The nearly four weeks of protests in Spain have contributed to political turmoil, leading to a snap general election being called for November 29.
Meanwhile, demonstrations over rising living costs have also taken place in France, Belgium and Italy.
Violence that erupted in France over the weekend on the sidelines of otherwise peaceful protests has raised concerns that similar unrest could spread to other countries facing comparable economic pressures.

title: El Salvadors Präsident kündigt an, Tausende Häftlinge freizulassen
content_c:
Präsident Nayib Bukele El Salvador kündigt an, Tausende Häftlinge freizulassen
Menschenrechtsorganisationen kritisieren, dass etwa die Hälfte der 90.000 Menschen in El Salvadors Gefängnissen unschuldig inhaftiert ist. Nun hat Präsident Bukele überraschend angekündigt, Tausende freizulassen.
Wenn Ingrid Escobar berichtet, wie sie den Beginn ihres Exils in Mexiko letztes Jahr erlebte, beginnt sie zu weinen.
"Mein Bruder ist Händler und hat Kosmetik aus Guatemala über die Grenze gebracht. Er war durch Zoll und Polizeikontrolle und wurde danach vom Militär dafür festgenommen, keine geschäftliche Rechnung bei sich zu haben. Eine Bagatelle, für die er in ein Hochsicherheitsgefängnis gebracht wurde."
Escobar ist Anwältin, Direktorin der Menschenrechtsorganisation Socorro Jurídico Humanitario, kurz SJH. Sie hat willkürliche Festnahmen, Folter und Hunderte Todesfälle in den Gefängnissen El Salvadors dokumentiert. Deshalb ist sie ins Visier der Regierung Nayib Bukeles geraten.
"Law-and-Order"-Politik
El Salvadors Präsident Bukele ist für seine harte "Law-and-Order"-Politik bekannt. Als vor vier Jahren die Gang MS-13 ein beispielloses Massaker verübte, hat er den Ausnahmezustand ausgerufen. Bis heute hat er etwa zwei Prozent der Bevölkerung des kleinen mittelamerikanischen Landes festnehmen lassen und beschuldigte sie, einer der Mara-Gangs anzugehören oder mit ihnen zu kooperieren.
Escobar wird polizeilich überwacht und bedroht. Als sie immer öfter von der Polizei besucht wird, weitere Menschenrechtsaktivisten festgenommen werden und sie an Krebs erkrankt, beschließt sie 2025, das Land zu verlassen.
"Es bestand das Risiko, dass sie mich festnehmen, und ich habe gedacht, ich gehe lieber ein paar Monate weg und überlege mir, wie ich meinem Bruder in Haft helfen kann. Ich habe mich im Ausland um meine Gesundheit gekümmert, mich operieren lassen", sagt Escobar. "Dann haben sie meinen Bruder umgebracht."
Sie wurde selbst Opfer des Systems, gegen das sie kämpfte. Allein am Todestag ihres Bruders wurden ihrer Aussage nach sechs Inhaftierte in derselben Zelle gefoltert, ein weiterer Mann ermordet. In der Kriminalstatistik El Salvadors tauchen sie nicht auf.
Überraschende Ankündigung von Bukele
Der Ausnahmezustand in El Salvador gilt seit 2022. Insgesamt über 90.000 Menschen sind in Hochsicherheitsgefängnissen untergebracht, laut Amnesty International teils fünf- bis sechsfach überbelegt. Die salvadorianische Menschenrechtsorganisation Socorro Jurídico Humanitario, kurz SJH, hat mindestens 554 Todesfälle in staatlichem Gewahrsam namentlich dokumentiert. Unter anderem wegen unterlassener medizinischer Hilfeleistung, Gewalt und Folter.
Präsident Bukele, der seine brutale Strategie bisher immer verteidigt hat, hat nun überraschend die Freilassung Tausender Menschen angekündigt. "Etwa die Hälfte der Häftlinge, die mit den Banden zusammengearbeitet haben, würde von einer vorzeitigen Freilassung profitieren. Sie sind weiterhin schuldig, darum sollen sie unter Auflagen freikommen."
Seine Regierung habe dafür eine Kommission eingerichtet, die parallel zum Justizsystem arbeitet. Für Ingrid Hausinger, Regionaldirektorin der Heinrich-Böll-Stiftung für die Region, bemerkenswert: Erstmals gebe Bukele damit offen zu, dass es keine Gewaltenteilung mehr in El Salvador gibt, kein unabhängiges Gericht entscheide also über die Haftfälle.
Laut Hausinger gibt es mehrere Gründe für Bukeles Ankündigung gerade jetzt: "Ich glaube, das kommt viel von dem internationalen Druck einerseits. Das zweite ist einfach dieses ganze System, das ist natürlich auch unglaublich schwer zu bewirtschaften und unglaublich teuer. Ich denke, nach mittlerweile fünf Jahren wird es schon ein bisschen unerträglich für die Regierung, das weiter zu finanzieren."
Anstehende Präsidentschaftswahlen
Außerdem: Ende Februar nächsten Jahres finden Präsidentschaftswahlen statt. Obwohl Bukele noch immer hohe Beliebtheitswerte hat und mit großer Wahrscheinlichkeit wiedergewinnt, wachse der Druck in der Bevölkerung.
"Es sind die Mütter von Gefangenen, die kein Recht, keinen Prozess hatten. Diese Bewegung hat mittlerweile schon viel internationale Lobbyarbeit gemacht, die sind sehr aktiv. Ich glaube, eine Art und Weise, diese Bewegung auch zum Schweigen zu bringen, ist, einige von diesen unschuldigen Menschen freizulassen", sagt Hausinger.
Bukele will zudem nicht öffentlich machen, dass viele der Insassen unschuldig sind, auch wenn er einmal zugab, dass etwa 8.000 Personen fälschlicherweise festgenommen wurden.
Viele Fragezeichen
Noch ist unklar, wer freigelassen wird. Und auch über den Zeitpunkt äußert sich der Präsident nicht. Deshalb glaubt die im mexikanischen Exil lebende Menschenrechtsanwältin Ingrid Escobar von SJH nicht daran, dass die Menschen freikommen.
"Alles, was er unserem Volk verkauft, ist heiße Luft. Er glaubt, er könne bestimmen, ob man Menschenrechte hat oder nicht," sagt Escobar. "Irgendwann, wenn diese Menschen freikommen, traumatisiert, moralisch wie körperlich missbraucht, werden sie die Institutionen hassen. Keiner hilft ihnen, sich wieder in die Gesellschaft zu integrieren."
Egal, ob Bukele jetzt das Versprechen hält und einen Teil der Gefangenen freilässt oder sie irgendwann nach dem Ende seiner Regierungszeit freikommen: El Salvador fehlten Programme zur Reintegration. Das Schlimmste wäre, befürchtet Escobar, wenn sich dann der Kreislauf der Gewalt wiederhole.

title: Britische Jets sollen Saudis vor Huthi-Angriffen schützen
content_c:
Britische Jets sollen Saudis vor Huthi-Attacken schützen
20. Oktober 2026
Großbritannien will Kampfjets entsenden, um Saudi-Arabien im Konflikt mit der pro-iranischen Huthi-Miliz im Jemen zu unterstützen. Der Einsatz sei Teil einer "zusätzlichen militärischen Verteidigungsunterstützung" für Riad, teilte das britische Verteidigungsministerium mit.
Britische Piloten würden "mit Typhoon-Kampfflugzeugen der Royal Air Force (RAF) defensive Luftabwehrmissionen fliegen, um den Schutz saudischer Städte und wichtiger nationaler Infrastruktur vor Luftangriffen zu unterstützen", hieß es weiter.
"Keine offensiven Angriffe"
Das Ministerium betonte, die Eurofighter-Kampfjets ergänzten die bereits in dem Land stationierten Kräfte. Sie würden "defensiv" eingesetzt; es seien keine "offensiven Angriffe gegen die Huthi" vorgesehen. Zudem plane Großbritannien, zum Transport von Ausrüstung innerhalb Saudi-Arabiens ein Militärtransportflugzeug zu entsenden.
"Die anhaltenden Angriffe der Huthi auf unseren Verbündeten Saudi-Arabien sind absolut verabscheuungswürdig", sagte der britische Verteidigungsminister Wes Streeting. Insbesondere kritisierte er die Attacken auf den Flughafen in der Hauptstadt Riad, die die Bereitschaft der Huthi zur Eskalation verdeutlichten.
Bedrohung am Bab al-Mandab
Saudi-Arabien wird fast täglich mit Raketen und Drohnen der Huthi-Miliz angegriffen. Die islamistischen Rebellen, die Teile des Jemens beherrschen, zielen auf Militärstützpunkte, Flughäfen und Energieinfrastruktur. Bei einem Angriff vor zehn Tagen auf den Flughafen von Riad waren 13 Menschen getötet und Hunderte verletzt worden. Zuvor hatten die Huthi die wichtige Ost-West-Pipeline angegriffen. Durch Vorstöße im Jemen hatten sie zudem die Küste nahe der Meerenge Bab al-Mandab unter ihre Kontrolle gebracht, von wo aus sie saudische Schiffe bedrohen.
Mit dem Beginn des US-israelischen Kriegs gegen den Iran Ende Februar ist auch der Konflikt zwischen den Huthi und der jemenitischen Regierung erneut eskaliert. Eine von Saudi-Arabien angeführte Militärkoalition unterstützt die international anerkannte jemenitische Regierung im Kampf gegen die vom Iran unterstützte Huthi-Miliz. Der Konflikt gilt als Stellvertreterkrieg zwischen den rivalisierenden Regionalmächten.
Nach Schätzungen von Nichtregierungsorganisationen wurden weit über 100.000 Menschen im Jemen durch unmittelbare Gewalteinwirkung getötet. Noch wesentlich mehr dürften durch die Folgen des Bürgerkrieges wie Hungersnöte und fehlende medizinische Versorgung gestorben sein. Mehr als 250.000 Menschen wurden laut den Vereinten Nationen vertrieben.
jj/gri (dpa, rtr)
Redaktionsschluss 17.45 Uhr (MESZ) - Dieser Artikel wird nicht weiter aktualisiert.
description: Die Flugzeuge vom Typ Eurofighter Typhoon können Drohnen und Raketen abfangen, die vom Jemen aus auf das arabische Königreich abgefeuert werden. Die Huthi-Miliz hatte den Saudis zuletzt schwer zugesetzt.

title: Україну охопить нова хвиля бабиного літа, але синоптики забили на сполох через небезпеку: які міста "накриє" (мапа)
content_c:
Україну охопить нова хвиля бабиного літа, але синоптики забили на сполох через небезпеку: які міста "накриє" (мапа)
Доки більшість областей насолоджується сонячним теплом, синоптики оголосили жовтий рівень небезпечності через густі ранкові тумани.
Найближчими днями в Україні утримуватиметься тепла погода, хоча в окремих регіонах можливі невеликі дощі та ранкові тумани.
Детальний прогноз погоди в Україні — читайте в матеріалі ТСН.ua.
Погода в Україні
Українська синоптикиня Наталка Діденко прогнозує теплу погоду в Україні 21 жовтня. Температура повітря вупродовж дня у більшості областей очікується від +13 до +18 градусів вище нуля. На заході та півдні країни буде подекуди від +18 до +22 градусів вище нуля.
«І такий температурний рахат-лукум триватиме до суботи й неділі. Якихось серйозних дощів не очікується, хіба періодично невеликі і дуже локально», — прогнозує вона.
Дощі 21 жовтня пройдуть на Сумщині, Чернігівщині, Полтавщині та подекуди у східних областях, також у кількох регіонах країни будуть тумани.
У Києві завтра очікується тепла погода з максимальною температурою повітря до +14…+15 градусів вище нуля, опадів не передбачається.
За словами синоптика Ігоря Кібальчича, до кінця жовтня в Україні утримуватиметься тепле та переважно сухе бабине літо з температурою на кілька градусів вищою за норму, передає Telegraf. Як прогнозує метеоролог, до 25 жовтня денне тепло сягатиме +13…+20 градусів вище нуля, а вночі буде в межах +6…+13 градусів тепла (лише на заході 23 жовтня похолоднішає до +8…+13 градусів тепла).
Кібальчич попереджає, що від 26 жовтня почнеться поступове зниження температури: нічні показники впадуть до +1…+7 градусів тепла, а на півночі можливі заморозки. Втім, удень залишатиметься помірно тепло — від +11 до +16 градусів вище нуля, а в Криму очікується до +19 градусів.

title: Оккупанты массированно атаковали Харьковскую область: погибли двое пожилых людей, повреждены дома
content_c:
В ночь на 21 октября оккупанты массированно атаковали беспилотниками село Коротыч в Харьковской области. Глава Харьковской областной государственной администрации Олег Синегубов в своем Telegram-канале сообщил, что в результате удара погибли 81-летняя женщина и 83-летний мужчина.
Отмечается, что еще у 11 человек, среди которых двухмесячный мальчик и восьмилетняя девочка, диагностировали острую реакцию на стресс. Всем пострадавшим оказали необходимую медицинскую помощь.
Синегубов отметил, что в результате атаки повреждения получили 13 частных домов и автомобиль. Также пожар уничтожил хозяйственную постройку. Экстренные службы работали в усиленном режиме, чтобы ликвидировать последствия российского удара.
Напомним, 20 октября российские войска нанесли ракетный удар по частному сектору Новобаварского района Харькова. В результате атаки девять местных жителей получили контузии и осколочные ранения. Также повреждения получили жилые дома и одно из предприятий.
Накануне российский беспилотник атаковал центральный парк Новой Водолаги в Харьковской области, где находилось много людей. В результате удара на месте погибли шесть человек, среди которых годовалый ребенок и 11-летняя девочка. Еще восемь взрослых и семь детей получили ранения различной степени тяжести.

title: Львівщина під ударами, атака на Бурштин, у Ковелі і Дубно горіли Епіцентри. Як Росія посилює атаки на захід України
content_c:
Львівщина під ударами, атака на Бурштин, у Ковелі і Дубно горіли Епіцентри. Як Росія посилює атаки на захід України
Впродовж ночі, ранку і дня під інтенсивною атакою Росії були і перебувають західні області України. Реактивні дрони атакували переважно об'єкти енергетики й цивільну інфраструктуру. У Ковелі та Дубно після атаки горіли гіпермаркети "Епіцентр", а біля Львова у Новояворівській громаді дрони кілька разів атакували енергетичний об'єкт - сусідні райони без світла.
Також є звіти влади про руйнування та поранених на Волині, Рівненщині і Тернопільщині.
Львів з півночі мав уже вісім повітряних тривог і в обід лунали вибухи - ППО збили реактивний шахед, який рухався у місто.
Якщо у серпні та вересні Росія кошмарила реактивними шахедами переважно Київ, то в останні дні виглядає, що значний акцент робиться і на західних регіонах.
Реактивні шахеди і далі хвилями рухаються на захід України, під ударом також інші регіони та Київ.
Львівщина
Львівщина пережила складну ніч, повідомив голова Львівської ОВА Максим Козицький.
"Найважливіше – без загиблих і постраждалих. Ворог атакував реактивними безпілотниками об'єкти енергетики в різних районах нашої області", - написав він.
На території Солонківської громади пошкоджені покрівлі житлового та двох дачних будинків.
Безпілотники рухалися на великій швидкості і часто змінювали курс, зазначив Козицький.
Ситуацію ускладнював туман, але "навіть за таких умов нашим воїнам вдалося ефективно відпрацювати по ворожих БпЛА", додав він.
Атака на Львівщину розпочалась пізно ввечері 19 жовтня і триває з невеликими перервами всю ніч, ранок і день. Близько 16 години дня на Львів рухаються нові дрони і у місті вже оголошували восьму тривогу за день.
При чому дрони один за одним залітали до Львова, довго кружляли просто над містом і далі атакували енергетичні об'єкти області.
Вночі Козицький вказав, що дрони двічі атакували енергетичний об'єкт біля Львова. Влада Новояворівська зранку визнала, що дрони двічі били по об'єкту критичної інфраструктури у їхній громаді.
20 жовтня дрони кілька разів повторно атакували Новояворівськ. Влада Новояворівська заявила про влучання у енергооб'єкт, частина міста опинилась без світла і води.
Влада каже, що сусідній Шептицький район теж не мав світла, але там проблеми полагодили.
Реактивні дрони вже кілька тижнів атакують Львів, у передмісті було багато руйнувань будинків та спалені автомобілі.
Тернопільщина
Голова Тернопільської ОДА Тарас Пастух також повідомив, що в ході нічних атак росіяни намагалися "цілеспрямовано вивести з ладу енергетичну інфраструктуру, залишити населення без світла і тепла".
В області зафіксовані пошкодження на трьох обʼєктах енергетики в Кременецькому районі та приватних домогосподарствах у Чортківському районі.
Інформації про потерпілих не надходило.
Волинь
Про "чергову важку ніч" повідомляють і з Волині.
"Фактично щогодини ворог спрямовував на нашу область реактивні БпЛА. Загалом у повітряному просторі Волині зафіксували близько 15 безпілотників, декілька з яких згодом вийшла на територію Львівської області", - повідомив голова Волинської ОДА Роман Романюк.
Основними цілями тут також стали об'єкти електроенергетики та цивільної інфраструктури.
Найбільше атак зазнав Ковель. Там пошкоджена приватна СТО, автостоянка вантажних автомобілів із напівпричепами. Також було влучання на території "Епіцентру", де постраждали складські приміщення.
Загиблих і травмованих в області немає.
Майже вся область зі світлом, додав Романюк.
Луцьк та Ковель останні тижні під постійним ударом Росії. У Ковелі Росія намагається паралізувати важливу залізничну гілку до Польщі.
Рівненщина
Через дронові атаки на Рівненщині у багатьох населених пунктах знеструмлення, повідомив голова місцевої ОДА Олександр Коваль.
Енергетики працюють над відновленням електропостачанням.
Коваль також повідомив про "тяжку ніч", однак зазначив, що "маємо багато знищених цілей".
Вдень Коваль повідомив, що на Рівненщині зазнав атаки торговельний центр.
За попередньою інформацією, троє людей поранені, з них двох – госпіталізували.
Триває пожежа, продукти горіння активно поширюються.
У соціальних мережає ширяться фотографії "Епіцентру" у Дубно, який горить після влучання дрона.
Джерела ВВС у владі вказують, що інформація про удар по вокзалу у Дубно помилкова - він просто розташований неподалік "Епіцентру". Сам об'єкт УЗ наразі цілий.
Росія цілеспрямовану нищить цю мережу у всіх регіонах країни.
Прикарпаття
Під атаками був і Бурштин на Прикарпатті, повідомляли Повітряні сили.
Вечері керівниця області Світлана Онищук розповіла, що Росія вдруге за сьогодні атакувала один з енергооб'єктів на Прикарпатті.
"На жаль, внаслідок останньої атаки є постраждалий. Йому надають необхідну медичну допомогу. На місці працюють відповідні служби, які ліквідовують наслідки ворожого удару", - каже вона.
У Бурштині на Прикарпатті розташований важливий енергетичний об'єкт.

title: Внаслідок російських обстрілів Дніпропетровщини було поранено людину і пошкоджено підприємство – ОВА
content_c:
Війська РФ у ніч на середу майже 30 разів атакували ракетами, безпілотниками та артилерією Дніпровський, Нікопольський і Синельниківський райони Дніпропетровської області, внаслідок чого одна людина дістала поранення та зафіксовані руйнування цивільної інфраструктури, повідомив голова Дніпропетровської обласної військової адміністрації Олександр Ганжа.
"На Нікопольщині потерпали райцентр, Марганецька, Покровська, Томаківська та Червоногригорівська громади. Пошкоджені приватні будинки, автівки, сільгосптехніка... У стані середньої тяжкості до лікарні доправили 50-річного чоловіка", – написав Ганжа у Телеграм.
За даними ОВА, у Нікопольському районі внаслідок обстрілів також виникли пожежі.
Крім того, у Синельниківському районі російські окупанти завдали ударів по районному центру та Миколаївській громаді, де пошкодили підприємство і приватний житловий будинок, спричинивши займання. У Дніпровському районі внаслідок ворожої атаки пошкоджено будівлю гуртожитку.

title: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say
content_c:
Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say
- Published
Sudan's army has been accused of launching several drone strikes that have reportedly killed more than 300 people, including dozens travelling to a funeral.
The death toll from strikes in two areas of West Kordofan state on Sunday evening was 150, sources told the Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict that erupted in 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
In Abyei, a disputed border area between Sudan and South Sudan, 153 people were killed when drones hit a market on Monday, the region's information minister said.
A military source told the BBC the army had carried out the Abyei attack, saying the market was a fuel supply site for the RSF.
The attack has raised tensions between South Sudan and Sudan, which jointly administer Abyei, as they both claim ownership to the oil-rich region in a dispute that has remained unresolved since South Sudan ceded in 2011.
South Sudan has summoned Sudan's ambassador to lodge a formal protest. There are fears the conflict could spill across the border.

title: Chancellor rejects calls to raise Capital Gains Tax in Budget
content_c:
Chancellor rejects calls to raise Capital Gains Tax in Budget
- Published
Chancellor John Healey has dismissed calls from some Labour MPs to increase Capital Gains Tax (CGT).
Cabinet ministers Wes Streeting and Louise Haigh both previously voiced support for raising CGT before Andy Burnham became prime minister in July.
Ahead of next week's Budget, as first reported by the Times, external, Healey is minded not to increase CGT - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value, such as shares in a company or properties which are not primary residences.
The move followed warnings that it could end up costing the government money if wealthy people leave the country or defer selling off assets.
If you pay income tax at the basic rate then CGT is charged at 18%. For higher and additional rate income tax payers, the CGT rate is 24%.
Last year, HMRC estimated, external that lifting the lower rate of CGT by 1% could raise £5m by 2028-9 but increasing the higher rate of CGT by 10% would reduce the Treasury's receipts by £3.6bn in 2028-9.
The amount raised could be reduced if people adapt their behaviour to the tax rise, for example by moving abroad or deciding not to sell a property.
The chancellor gave an indication of his approach last month in a speech when he spoke about the importance of businesses and self-employed people making profits.
"I want to see this country as a country of wealth creation. I want our government decisions and policies to raise the levels of confidence, and investment, and profit in British business," Healey said.
Burnham has faced warnings against lifting CGT. His former adviser and Goldman Sachs Chief Economist Lord Jim O'Neill suggested it would send "the wrong message to business".
But influential Labour figures had pushed for equalising CGT and income tax, with the former generally attracting a lower tax rate.
Louise Haigh, a key ally of the prime minister, had suggested capital gains should go up to be closer to income tax, before she became Burnham's first secretary of state.
In an article for the Renewal journal,, external Haigh argued that raising CGT would "shift the taxation burden away from punishing work, and towards unproductive capital accumulation which does little to grow the everyday economy".
She said this could be accompanied by measures to ensure that "genuine investment returns are not penalised".
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called for a "wealth tax that works" in May, shortly after resigning as a minister in former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government.
He had argued that equalising CGT with income tax would address an unfair system that was "penalising work".
Healey had already ruled out levelling the two tax rates, according to a report in the Financial Times last week, external.
Asked about the government's plans for CGT on BBC Breakfast, Communities Secretary Angela Rayner would not speculate on the Budget.
Pressed over whether rejecting calls to increase the tax was a win for the rich, she said the government had already taken steps to give people "breathing space" and help with the cost of living.
It comes after senior banking executives told the BBC they expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector. UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes.
Healey is due to set out his tax and spending plans at his first Budget on 28 October, against the backdrop of the US-Iran war which has led to rising prices.
The chancellor is under pressure to find measures to ease the cost of living and fund an increase for defence at his spending review next year.
The chancellor's options for raising money are limited as Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged not to increase income tax, National Insurance and VAT, the three big revenue raisers.
The government is also restricted in how much it can borrow due to its self-imposed rules on debt.
- What is the Budget and what could be in it? 
  - Published21 hours ago
- Labour will not have the courage to cut spending, says Badenoch 
  - Published15 hours ago
- Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget 
  - Published4 days ago
In a pre-Budget speech on Tuesday, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch urged the government to cut spending and reduce its borrowing.
She said the prime minister and the chancellor should "live within our means" and pointed to her party's plan to save £70bn in cuts, including to welfare and overseas development aid.
Badenoch told an audience in central London that Labour would not "find the courage" to cut spending.
She said the chancellor wanted to deliver a "nothing to see here Budget" but added: "Britain cannot afford to do as little as possible."
The Liberal Democrats have said the government could raise £14bn partly by introducing a windfall tax on the profits of banks.
The party's deputy leader Daisy Cooper said the money could go towards cutting fuel duty, rail and bus fares and VAT for hospitality businesses.

title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wins dismissal of sister's lawsuit
content_c:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wins dismissal of sister's lawsuit
- Published
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman has won a dismissal of a lawsuit brought against him by his sister that claimed he had sexually abused her more than two decades ago.
A US district judge dismissed the case after Ann Altman had refused to attend an independent medical examination, adding she was warned a failure to do so would result in the case being thrown out.
Ann Altman had claimed the OpenAI founder had regularly sexually abused her between 1997 and 2006. Sam Altman has denied those accusations.
The Altman family has said Ann Altman has mental health challenges and they have supported her financially, adding the claims were made as she continued to demand more funds.
District Judge Zachary Bluestone said that despite multiple accommodations and multiple opportunities to do so, Ann Altman did not appear for an independent medical exam on three separate occasions, and "failed to meaningfully prosecute her case".
"Because Annie has continued to violate her discovery obligations and forced this case to a halt through her intransigence, the Court has run out of options and, thus, dismisses her claims with prejudice," he said in his written order.
The case was filed on 6 January 2025 in the Eastern District of Missouri.
In it, Ann Altman claimed that her older brother Sam Altman began abusing her when she was three, and he was 12.
However, in a joint statement released by Sam Altman along with his mother and two brothers at the time, the family said they were concerned for Ann Altman's wellbeing and have spent years trying to support her financially and to look after her wellbeing.
The family said she receives monthly financial support, and her bills and rent were also covered, while also trying to assist with medical help.
The statement said her claims against Sam Altman had changed drastically over time, but all of those claims were "utterly untrue".
Sam Altman is the co-founder of OpenAI, which launched its popular ChatGPT artificial intelligence chatbot in 2022.
If you've been affected by the issues in this story, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line.

title: Giving £2 a day to people in the Amazon helps protect rainforest, pilot project finds
content_c:
A pioneering project to provide Indigenous people in the Peruvian Amazon with an unconditional basic income has contributed to the protection of the rainforest, according to a study.
The analysis from the University of Bath is expected to contribute to a growing debate about the role of direct payments to communities that maintain globally important ecosystems.
A two-year pilot managed by the UK-based charity Cool Earth gave 211 people in three communities in Peru’s Asháninka region six cash transfers of 1,032 Peruvian soles each – roughly equivalent to £2 a day – to spend as they wished.
Over the course of the trial, researchers found almost 90% of participants adopted environmentally beneficial practices, such as collective reforestation, restoration of critical water sources and reductions of forest burning.
They also noted a reduction in food insecurity, which can sometimes prompt forest people to start logging or become involved in environmental crimes. Households unable to afford nutritious food fell from 73% to 26%.
Another reported benefit was reduced migration, with the share of participants forced to leave their homes to find work falling from 43% to 18%. Researchers said this allowed more people to remain and protect the forest.
Dr Nick Langridge, a co-author of the report, said: “The findings suggest that when communities have greater security and autonomy, they are better able to protect the ecosystems they depend on.”
There is increasing recognition of the importance of Indigenous stewardship of the Amazon and other biomes that sequester carbon, shelter biodiversity and provide vital ecological services to the planet. But this role is increasingly difficult as Indigenous lands are threatened by miners, loggers, farmers and land grabbers, and as many of the young people of these often economically poor communities are exposed to the internet or lured away to wealthier cities.
How to sustain, encourage and reward Indigenous stewardship is a hot debate in the international aid and environmental community. Many previous payment schemes came with strings attached, such as the Brazilian government’s bolsa família, which has child education obligations, or bolsa verde, which has conservation activity requirements.
The authors of the new study say the project – which was drawn up with local women’s groups – is the first to offer an unconditional basic income to an Indigenous community in the Amazon.
The lead author, Dr Neil Howard, said: “All of this helps ethical conservation. The incentive to exploit or abandon land is diminished, and people are put front and centre with respect and dignity, which contrasts sharply with the colonial history of conservation and Indigenous policy.”
To boost the impact, the project delivered a voluntary “cash plus” complementary programme of community-led education on finance, conservation and climate change.
Other academics are more cautious about the environmental impacts of cash transfers, pointing out that similar studies elsewhere have found they can lead to an increase in deforestation as people use the extra cash to expand agriculture.
In some parts of the Amazon, cash payments are used to buy motorbikes and cars, which increases demand for more roads. There are also reports of Indigenous communities becoming more exposed to drugs when they visit cities to collect transfers.
The authors of the new report acknowledge that wider research is needed on the ecological impacts of unconditional basic income. Their two-year study was small, covering little over 500 hectares (1,235 acres) of forest. They did not measure changes in vegetation or soil quality, nor account for the influence of any separate projects that might have been affecting community behaviour.
Despite these limitations, they say the early results have excited the cash-for-conservation network of civil society organisations.
“Yes, this is an experimental pilot and and we could do with something much larger,” Howard said. “But this is very pioneering. My hope is that the trade-off between scale and innovation tips in this direction.”

title: My late wife Jo Cox was murdered in her constituency in 2016. The alleged attack on Helen Haines is a punch to the gut | Brendan Cox
content_c:
It’s never a good sign when you turn on your phone to find a dozen messages asking if you are OK. For reasons you will come to understand, I only get those messages when something awful has happened.
So on Monday, when I came out of an all-day meeting on antisemitism and picked up the messages from friends, I clicked across to check the news with real dread. The last time I’d received a similar barrage of messages was when former UK MP Ann Widdecombe was killed earlier this year.
As I read the news about the alleged attack on Australian MP Helen Haines, the dread I felt was followed by what I can best describe as a punch to the gut. A wave of shock. Deep sorrow. The despair that another elected representative had been so brutally injured.
Jo Cox MP, my late wife, was murdered in 2016 in her constituency in Yorkshire, England by a far-right extremist as she went about her constituency work.
Helen’s story reminded me of what happened to Jo. Both incidents took place in a small town far from the corridors of power. Helen, like Jo, clearly has a deep connection with her community. Even their names connected them (Jo’s first name was Helen – though she always used Jo as her main name).
When something like this happens it’s impossible not to feel yourself back in the moment of your own loss. My immediate reaction was to hope to God she survives – I remembered how I prayed the same as I heard the news about Jo’s attack.
I quickly worried about her family, the impact on them, and immediately recalled the impact on mine.
And then of course you worry about the impact on the country, its democracy and the values that underpin it.

It’s never a good sign when you turn on your phone to find a dozen messages asking if you are OK. For reasons you will come to understand, I only get those messages when something awful has happened.

Jo Cox MP, my late wife, was murdered in 2016 in her constituency in Yorkshire, England by a far-right extremist as she went about her constituency work.

title: AfD's Alice Weidel to unveil plan to cut EU powers — report
content_c:
AfD's Alice Weidel to unveil plan to cut EU powers — report
October 21, 2026
Alice Weidel, the co-leader of Germany's far-right AfD, is expected to present her party's policy for the EU at the European Parliament on Wednesday.
According to a report from news outlet Politico, the AfD policy paper on the EU does not seek to exit the bloc or the eurozone at first.
The party rather wants to downsize the EU's powers and budget.
What's in the AfD policy paper?
Instead of direct European Parliament elections, the AfD would like to see delegates appointed by national parliaments.
The AfD would also limit the scope of the European Commission to purely administrative tasks and supplant the European Court of Justice with an arbitration tribunal.
The far right party would threaten to slash Germany's contributions to the EU budget.
Germany under the AfD would seek exemptions from EU regulations regarding issues such as migration and social policy. The AfD may also seek opt-outs of other areas such as agriculture and financial policies.
If the EU would not bend to the AfD's demands for reform, the party would then seek a German referendum on EU membership.
A referendum would be unrealistic, as it would require a constitutional amendment to the German Basic Law to take place. An amendment would require a two-thirds majority vote in both the Bundestag and upper house Bundesrat — an extremely high threshold to meet.
AfD eyes victory in next federal elections in 2029
The AfD hopes that it can implement its EU policies in 2029, when the next German and European elections will take place.
Recent German federal election surveys show the AfD in first place but it would have to form a coalition with another partner to establish a ruling majority government. That's difficult when other parties such as the conservative Christian Democratic Union refuse to have any cooperation with the AfD as part of a "firewall" policy.
Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

title: Nigeria bestätigt ersten Ebola-Fall
content_c:
Bundibugyo-Variante Nigeria bestätigt ersten Ebola-Fall
Bislang waren drei afrikanische Länder von dem aktuellen Ebola-Ausbruch betroffen, nun meldet auch Nigeria einen Fall. Eine Frau sei in der Hauptstadt Abuja in Behandlung, so die Behörden. Nigeria ist das bevölkerungsreichste Land auf dem Kontinent.
In Afrikas bevölkerungsreichstem Land Nigeria ist der erste Fall einer Ebola-Infektion bestätigt worden. Die Patientin sei kürzlich per Flugzeug aus Uganda eingereist und für mehrere Tage in einem Privatkrankenhaus im Gebiet der Hauptstadt Abuja behandelt worden, teilte das Gesundheitsministerium des westafrikanischen Landes mit.
Laborergebnisse hätten nun ergeben, dass die Frau mit dem Ebola-Virus des Bundibugyo-Stammes infiziert sei. Sie befinde sich nach Angaben des Ministeriums in Isolation und werde medizinisch versorgt. Die Ermittlung von Personen, die mit der Patientin in Kontakt standen, habe begonnen. Bisher seien 44 Kontakte identifiziert worden, darunter medizinisches Personal, andere Patienten, Pflegekräfte sowie Reisekontakte.
Die Regierung rief alle öffentlichen und privaten Gesundheitseinrichtungen in dem Land mit rund 220 Millionen Einwohnern zu "höchster Wachsamkeit" auf.
Insgesamt vier afrikanische Länder betroffen
Der aktuelle Ebola-Ausbruch hatte Mitte Mai in der Demokratischen Republik Kongo begonnen. Nigeria ist inzwischen das vierte afrikanische Land, in dem Fälle der Bundibugyo-Variante gemeldet wurden. Im zentralafrikanischen Kongo wurden nach Angaben der Gesundheitsbehörde aktuell 9.552 Fälle und 4.602 Todesfälle registriert.
Im ostafrikanischen Kenia sind derzeit acht Ebola-Fälle, darunter ein Todesfall, bekannt. Auch in Uganda, das an den Kongo sowie an Kenia grenzt, gab es insgesamt 20 bestätigte Ebola-Fälle, die auf einen Patienten aus dem Kongo zurückgeführt wurden. Zwei Patienten starben. Uganda verkündete Ende August jedoch das Ende seines Ebola-Ausbruchs, nachdem über 42 Tage kein neuer Fall erfasst wurde.

title: Rot-Grün-Rot in Berlin nimmt Konturen an - trotz heftiger Kritik
content_c:
Rot-Grün-Rot in Berlin nimmt Konturen an - trotz heftiger Kritik
20. Oktober 2026
Dass in der deutschen Hauptstadt Berlin künftig eine rot-grün-rote Koalition regiert, wird wahrscheinlicher. Etwas über vier Wochen sind seit der Wahl zum Berliner Abgeordnetenhaus am 20. September vergangen. Zweimal standen die ersten vorsichtigen Gespräche der drei Parteien, Sondierungen genannt, vor dem Scheitern.
Dann einigten sich alle Beteiligten am vergangenen Wochenende auf formale und ernsthafte Gespräche über eine Koalition. Zu Beginn der Woche stimmten die Sozialdemokraten und die Grünen dieser Einigung ihrer Unterhändler zu.
Bei den Linken muss erst noch ein Parteitag in zwei Wochen für Koalitionsgespräche votieren. Erst in zwei Wochen deshalb, weil in Berlin gerade Herbstferien sind.
Die Linke hatte die Wahl vor der CDU, der AfD, den Grünen und der SPD gewonnen. Sie könnte mit ihrer Spitzenkandidatin Erif Eralp bald die Regierende Bürgermeisterin stellen, falls die Koalitionsgespräche erfolgreich sind.
Bundeskanzler Merz: Bündnis wäre Belastung für die Bundesregierung
Die größte Metropole in Deutschland, Berlin mit seinen knapp vier Millionen Einwohnern, regiert von einem Bündnis eher linker Parteien? Das hat zu heftigen Reaktionen vor allem bei den Konservativen geführt. Denn in der Bundesregierung führt Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz (CDU) ein Bündnis mit den Sozialdemokraten, die sich nun in der Hauptstadt für eine andere politische Richtung entschieden haben.
Besonders pikant: Auch CDU, Grüne und SPD hätten zusammen im Berliner Stadtparlament eine Mehrheit. Die Hauptstadt ist eines der 16 Bundesländer, spricht damit über die zweite deutsche Kammer, den Bundesrat, auch in der nationalen Politik mit. Was die Brisanz noch erhöht.
So äußerte sich Merz am Wochenende auf dem Treffen der CDU/CSU-Nachwuchsgruppe "Junge Union" in Bonn recht drastisch über das möglich neue Bündnis in Berlin: Die Gespräche mit "dieser linksradikalen Partei" müssten sofort beendet werden, rief Merz erregt in den Saal. Und weiter: "Hört auf damit, diesen Weg zu gehen." Andernfalls sei das auch eine Belastung für die schwarz-rote Koalition im Bund.
Die Junge Union präsentierte derweil ein Banner mit der Aufschrift "Nie wieder ist jetzt", eine Formulierung , die sonst bei Warnungen vor der in Teilen rechtsextremen "Alternative für Deutschland" (AfD) benutzt wird. Mit dem "Nie wieder" ist die Zeit des Nationalsozialismus in Deutschland zwischen 1933 und 1945 gemeint.
Ökonom Marcel Fratzscher warnt vor Panikmache
Die Linke hatte die Wahl vor allem mit ihrer Kritik an den hohen Mieten in Berlin gewonnen. Alle drei möglichen Regierungspartner streben jetzt eine "Vergesellschaftung" von rund 160.000 Wohnungen an, die aus privatem Besitz in Landesbesitz wechseln sollen. Kalkuliert wird mit einer Entschädigung von rund 17 Milliarden Euro. Ob das rechtlich durchsetzbar ist, ist offen.
Diese Pläne hat Bundeswirtschaftsministerin Katherina Reiche (CDU) heftig kritisiert. Das mögliche neue Dreier-Bündnis in Berlin sei eine "Gefahr für den Standort", die weit über Berlin hinausgehe.
Dazu sagte der Ökonom Marcel Fratzscher im Radio des "Rundfunk Berlin-Brandenburg" (rbb) am Dienstag: "Ich will da jetzt nicht die einzelnen Positionen der Linken verteidigen, aber ich halte diese Panikmache für übertrieben." Fratzscher ist Präsident des Deutschen Instituts für Wirtschaftsforschung (DIW).
Merz: "Wir stemmen uns gegen wachsenden Antisemitismus in Deutschland"
Umstritten war vor und nach der Wahl die Haltung der Linken zum Antisemitismus. Die Linken hatten in den vergangenen Jahren starken Zulauf von vielen jungen Berlinern, auch aus migrantischen Gruppen. Nicht wenige von ihnen sind entschiedene Kritiker Israels, sie fordern einen palästinensischen Staat, einige leugnen das Existenzrecht Israels.
Spitzenkandidatin Elif Eralp hat sich stets gegen jede Form des Antisemitismus gewandt. Dennoch fürchten einige, dass dieses Thema die künftige Regierungsarbeit belasten könnte.
Auch auf diese Kontroverse in Berlin ging Merz beim Treffen der "Jungen Union" ein. Er sagte: "Wir bekennen uns zum Existenzrecht Israels, und das ist unerschütterlich. Wir stemmen uns gegen einen wachsenden Antisemitismus in Deutschland."
Und weiter: "Gerade an diesem Tag sollen diese unverhandelbaren Grundsätze unseres Gemeinwesens allen Ernstes verhandelt werden, sollen in Teilen zur Disposition gestellt werden für ein Regierungsbündnis mitten in unserer Hauptstadt?"
"Rot-Grün-Rot" in zwei weiteren Bundesländern
Der Stadtstaat Bremen ist ein weiteres der 16 Bundesländer - und wird schon länger von SPD, Linken und Grünen regiert. Bremens Bürgermeister Andreas Bovenschulte (SPD) sagte dem Berliner "Tagesspiegel" zur Debatte über die politische Zukunft in der Hauptstadt: "Ich rufe die Union auf, aus ihrem völlig irrationalen und unverantwortlichen Hysterie-Modus auszusteigen." CDU und CSU, so der SPD-Politiker, würden "die inhaltliche Ablehnung von politischen Positionen in einen Topf mit dem Widerstand gegen verfassungsfeindlichen Extremismus" werfen.
Auch im nordöstlichen Bundesland Mecklenburg-Vorpommern wurde am 20. September gewählt, auch dort verhandeln Sozialdemokraten, Linke und Grüne gerade über eine Koalition. Anders als in Berlin geht das dort weitgehend geräuschlos über die Bühne.
description: SPD und Grüne in der Hauptstadt stimmen für Koalitionsgespräche, die Linke will bald folgen. Die heftige Kritik vor allem der Konservativen hält an, vor allem an den Plänen zur Wohnungspolitik.
