title: Haitian migrants changed this US town - Trump's deportation drive is reshaping it again
content_c:
Haitian migrants changed this US town - Trump's deportation drive is reshaping it again
- Published
In this closely fought midterm election campaign, the small town of Springfield, Ohio, has become a symbol of modern America. But it is a symbol that changes dramatically depending on who is describing it.
To President Donald Trump, Springfield crystallises America's problems due to years of unchecked immigration. He once echoed a false claim that Haitian immigrants were eating pets here. Today, he says his mass deportation drive means its people are "getting their town back".
But to others, Springfield represents a well-known cycle in the story of modern America. The decline of traditional industry, followed by a spike in immigration fuelled by cheap housing and low-paid labour. It is a familiar tale across the country.
This story contains some distressing details
Pierre Damas Bel, 20, arrived in Springfield to join his father and stepmother in 2024.
He fled his native Haiti, which was gripped by political instability and gang warfare. He entered the US with the government's permission under a now-defunct Biden-era programme for migrants waiting in Mexico.
Bel, according to a family friend, then received a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS), which gives vetted individuals the right to live and work in the United States.
TPS usually lasts 18 months but is routinely rolled over, often for years, if the danger remains in the affected country.
Bel aspired to build a life in America, the friend said. He was an honours student, talented athlete and cadet in a high school programme training students to become officers in the US Armed Forces.
But in June, the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for some 350,000 Haitians in the US.
Bel was told to report to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) field office where he was fitted with an ankle monitor which is used to track migrants facing deportation.
He wrote on Instagram that he felt "shame and humiliation" at having to wear the tag. And on 31 August, he parked his car on the side of a highway near Springfield, walked into oncoming traffic and was killed.
His family blamed his death on his feelings at having to wear the ankle monitor.
The Department for Homeland Security (DHS) did not respond to questions from the BBC about Bel's case. ICE has previously rejected "any attempt to blame ICE for the death".
"Remaining in the country illegally, while fighting removal, is a choice. Leaving with a free flight home and $2,600 is also a choice," a spokesperson told US media earlier this year when asked about the case.
In the weeks before his death, Bel attended a Springfield support centre for Haitians facing deportation.
Its co-founder, Viles Dorsainvil, told the BBC that Bel had been in the process of filing a motion asking ICE to remove the tag.
"He went twice to the ICE facilities… begging them to remove the ankle monitor," he said. "He did everything right to be here until they put the tag on him."
In total, more than a million immigrants from 13 countries have had TPS terminated by the Trump administration. The changes meant many went from being legal to unauthorised migrants overnight.
In 2024, Trump made securing the border and the mass deportation of undocumented migrants core pledges in his election campaign. Polls suggest the border policy continues to have strong support among Republicans, but the nature of his immigration enforcement campaign has seen a drop in backing this year.
Ohio has become a swing state in the coming midterm Congressional elections, and one of two Republican-held Senate seats is up for grabs. Trump has visited the state twice already in an attempt to rally turnout and counter a slide in his approval ratings.
At a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, earlier this month, Trump returned to the topic of Springfield.
"You have a little town, beautiful little town in Ohio where they dropped about 35,000 Haitians. Well, they're being taken out and they're almost going to be gone and we're giving their town back," he said to cheers.
The Trump administration first announced in June 2025 that it would be removing the TPS for Haitians, and the ensuing legal battle went all the way to the Supreme Court, which ruled in its favour in the summer.
"The T in TPS stands for TEMPORARY, yet many of these designations became de facto amnesty," James Percival, the general counsel for the Department of Homeland Security, said after the court's ruling. "This is a win for the rule of law and common sense."
In a social media post in August, the Department of Homeland Security posted a video of Haitians in chains wearing white uniforms being led onto a deportation flight. The video, accompanied by jaunty music, told Haitians whose TPS had expired to "LEAVE IMMEDIATELY".
The Trump administration has said it is conducting law enforcement operations in the town to keep Americans safe. It has also argued that Haiti is safe enough to return to.
The country is subject to the US State Department's highest Level 4 "Do Not Travel" danger warning.
The signs of decades of economic decline are still visible in Springfield, through shuttered factories and boarded up homes.
This part of the American Midwest was hit badly by last century's de-industrialisation, when those laid off from its once prolific factories sought work on the coasts or migrated to warmer, southern states.
Within the last five years, a Haitian population estimated to be around 20,000 strong arrived in the town. Many fled the devastating earthquake in 2010. Others left Haiti in 2021 during the violence and unrest that followed President Jovenel Moise's assassination.
It meant Springfield's population increased rapidly. With their legal status under TPS, many Haitians took on low-paid jobs in factories and distribution warehouses.
Rick Johnson, who served in the Marines, has a porch adorned with flags. The Stars and Stripes flutter close to a banner for the US Navy and another for the Marine Corps.
Johnson's wife served in the Navy while he was in the Marines at Camp Pendleton in California. Outside of his service, he has lived in Springfield his whole life. He made it clear he is a strong supporter of ICE's deportation drive.
"You get where we're coming from," he said. "We love America, we love Americans - any kind of Americans, but you kind of have to be American."
Johnson moved into this neighbourhood a decade ago, but he said the loss of industry has left much of it empty. "They've torn down every house around me, I don't really have any neighbours," he said. "The only neighbours I have are Haitians right here and they don't really bother me."
They moved in around four years ago, Johnson added, "but there's a lot of them". He referenced "the driving problems".
This is a view shared by other residents in Springfield - a perception that traffic accidents increased after the Haitian community arrived.
In 2023, an 11-year-old boy, Aiden Clark, was killed when his school bus overturned in a crash with a minivan. The van driver, Herman Joseph, originally from Haiti, did not have a valid US driver's licence and was jailed.
Aiden's father, Nathan Clark, later spoke at a Springfield City Commission meeting where he denounced politicians for using his son's death as a "political tool" to fuel anti-immigrant sentiment, saying his son was accidentally killed.
Johnson's concern is about the numbers and the speed of change. "Really it's the amount of them," he told the BBC. "If you come here you [should] come here legally. The Temporary Protected Status is done… it's time to go."
At a nearby grocery store run by Paschur Castelly, who left Haiti 20 years ago, most of the shelves are empty, except for those stocking religious candles and framed pictures of Catholic saints popular with this devout community.
"I can't purchase new merchandise because I don't have people coming in," he said.
"So, our communities, we have doctors, we have engineers… we came here to get a better life, to help our family in Haiti, you know? Our country doesn't offer us security."
After 20 minutes in the store, the first customer arrived. The man, who asked to remain anonymous, said he had been a warehouse worker for three years.
But like others who have lost TPS, it is likely to mean he has also lost the right to work.
As he chatted with Castelly, he pulled up his right trouser leg and revealed a large ankle monitor.
ICE has said these are part of its Alternatives to Detention programme. "I was given a choice, wear the ankle monitor and report in every two weeks, or sign my deportation order," he said.
As we left the store, Castelly closed the door which he now keeps locked. When a neighbour spotted us and feared an ICE raid, she shouted over to ask if Castelly was okay.
It was a sign of just how much this town remains a symbol - of two versions of America - years after Trump thrust it into the national spotlight, and weeks before voters head to the polls to shape the remainder of his presidency.
With additional reporting by Gringo Wotshela

title: Who is Chancellor John Healey? Labour veteran who quit as defence secretary
content_c:
Who is Chancellor John Healey? Labour veteran who quit as defence secretary
- Published
Andy Burnham's decision to appoint John Healey to the crucial role of chancellor of the exchequer was the rarest of things at Westminster - a genuine surprise.
It's not that the 66-year-old lacked experience or credibility - just that he had not been seen as a likely contender, with all the speculation about who would replace Rachel Reeves centring on more high-profile figures.
Healey had flown under the radar since his explosive resignation as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June this year.
His assessment of the government's defence investment plan - that it fell "well short of what is required for defence and the country at this dangerous time" - was devastating and undoubtedly hastened Sir Keir's departure from Downing Street.
But his resignation letter also included pointed criticism of Reeves's Treasury, which he said had been "unwilling" to "commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country at this time of rising threats".
Now he is in the Treasury hot seat and under pressure to spell out how he will get defence spending up to 3% of national income, at the same time as cutting government borrowing costs and tackling the cost of living.
Like his predecessor, he faces the difficult balancing act of keeping Labour MPs happy without spooking the financial markets, while delivering on the government's key priorities.
Never the flashiest of politicians, his early speeches as chancellor have been focused on stressing his commitment to fiscal discipline and cutting the welfare bill, as well as banging the drum for Burnham's plan to "reindustrialise" Britain.
But he did show his lighter side in a social media video with the prime minister, which saw "Andy and John" bantering about twiglets and scampi fries in the pub., external
"I will always stand by my political choices as chancellor, including pork scratchings as the best pub snack," he revealed on X.
- What is the Budget and what could be in it? 
  - Published21 hours ago
- Best thing we can offer young people is a job, not benefits, says chancellor 
  - Published28 September
The softly-spoken Yorkshireman has a remarkable record as someone who has been on the Labour frontbench almost continuously since 2001.
Born in Wakefield in 1960 and educated at Lady Lumley's Comprehensive School, Pickering, and Peter's School in York, he studied social and political science at Christ's College, Cambridge.
Before entering politics, he worked as a journalist, briefly editing Parliament's in-house magazine The House, before becoming a disability rights campaigner and trade union official.
He is married and has one son.
He first came into Parliament in Tony Blair's landslide general election in 1997 as MP for Wentworth, a former mining area north of Sheffield, which following boundary changes is now Rawmarsh and Conisbrough.
He retained the seat with a majority of 6,908 in the 2024 general election, with a Reform UK candidate in second place.
In the early 2000s, he held a string of ministerial posts, including housing, local government in the Blair and Gordon Brown governments.
He spent five years at Brown's Treasury where he oversaw policies such as the child trust funds and attempts to regenerate and devolve power - the Regional Development Agencies, later scrapped by the coalition government.
Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson earlier this month, Healey said: "The Treasury's a paradox. You have some of the very best and brightest officials in the Treasury, but you have too often a Treasury orthodox that's a dead hand on dynamic government."
He added that maintaining financial stability was a key function of the Treasury but "also it can and it has to drive economic growth, raise levels of productivity, support business competition, investment for the for the future".
And he claimed the department "was in denial about the commitment that the UK has rightly made to NATO and to our people" to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP, which would not come until 2034/35 under current plans.
"The Treasury still often sees defence as a drain on public spending and not the driver of economic growth that we've demonstrated in two years," he told Nick Robinson.
Healey's other area of expertise is housing. He served as shadow housing secretary when Jeremy Corbyn was Labour leader, despite supporting a failed attempt to oust Corbyn in 2016.
When Sir Keir was elected Labour leader in 2020, he made Healey shadow defence secretary, becoming defence secretary when Labour came to power four years later.
Healey was a staunch supporter of Ukraine in its war with Russia and made several trips to the country to meet President Zelensky.
At his first meeting with Nato allies, in September 2024, he said he was "confident" Labour could honour a commitment to increase defence spending and "make the decisions that allow us to set out a long-term plan to make our forces better equipped to fight and to deter the threats we face".
Healey also drove investment in housing for armed forces families, with a £9bn spending plan.
Despite his low key style, he proved capable of delivering stern warnings to the UK's enemies.
In April this year, he delivered a message to Russian President Vladimir Putin, in a briefing on "covert" operations by Russian sumbmarines, saying: "We see you.
"We see your activity over our cables and our pipelines, and you should know that any attempt to damage them will not be tolerated and will have serious consequences."
Following the announcement of the defence investment plan, he condemned what he called "Treasury trickery" and the lack of clarity on what new money the Ministry of Defence would get.
Healey also made clear that he wanted a clear plan to increase UK defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030.
He is not expected to do that in his first Budget, with key spending decisions set to be unveiled next year.
But the tax and spending decisions he does announce on 28 October will still have a huge impact on the success or failure of the fledgling Burnham administration.

Born in Wakefield in 1960 and educated at Lady Lumley's Comprehensive School, Pickering, and Peter's School in York, he studied social and political science at Christ's College, Cambridge.
Before entering politics, he worked as a journalist, briefly editing Parliament's in-house magazine The House, before becoming a disability rights campaigner and trade union official.
He is married and has one son.
He first came into Parliament in Tony Blair's landslide general election in 1997 as MP for Wentworth, a former mining area north of Sheffield, which following boundary changes is now Rawmarsh and Conisbrough.
He retained the seat with a majority of 6,908 in the 2024 general election, with a Reform UK candidate in second place.
In the early 2000s, he held a string of ministerial posts, including housing, local government in the Blair and Gordon Brown governments.
He spent five years at Brown's Treasury where he oversaw policies such as the child trust funds and attempts to regenerate and devolve power - the Regional Development Agencies, later scrapped by the coalition government.
Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson earlier this month, Healey said: "The Treasury's a paradox. You have some of the very best and brightest officials in the Treasury, but you have too often a Treasury orthodox that's a dead hand on dynamic government."
He added that maintaining financial stability was a key function of the Treasury but "also it can and it has to drive economic growth, raise levels of productivity, support business competition, investment for the for the future".
And he claimed the department "was in denial about the commitment that the UK has rightly made to NATO and to our people" to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP, which would not come until 2034/35 under current plans.
"The Treasury still often sees defence as a drain on public spending and not the driver of economic growth that we've demonstrated in two years," he told Nick Robinson.
Healey's other area of expertise is housing. He served as shadow housing secretary when Jeremy Corbyn was Labour leader, despite supporting a failed attempt to oust Corbyn in 2016.
When Sir Keir was elected Labour leader in 2020, he made Healey shadow defence secretary, becoming defence secretary when Labour came to power four years later.
Healey was a staunch supporter of Ukraine in its war with Russia and made several trips to the country to meet President Zelensky.
At his first meeting with Nato allies, in September 2024, he said he was "confident" Labour could honour a commitment to increase defence spending and "make the decisions that allow us to set out a long-term plan to make our forces better equipped to fight and to deter the threats we face".
Healey also drove investment in housing for armed forces families, with a £9bn spending plan.
Despite his low key style, he proved capable of delivering stern warnings to the UK's enemies.
In April this year, he delivered a message to Russian President Vladimir Putin, in a briefing on "covert" operations by Russian sumbmarines, saying: "We see you.
"We see your activity over our cables and our pipelines, and you should know that any attempt to damage them will not be tolerated and will have serious consequences."
Following the announcement of the defence investment plan, he condemned what he called "Treasury trickery" and the lack of clarity on what new money the Ministry of Defence would get.
Healey also made clear that he wanted a clear plan to increase UK defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030.
He is not expected to do that in his first Budget, with key spending decisions set to be unveiled next year.
But the tax and spending decisions he does announce on 28 October will still have a huge impact on the success or failure of the fledgling Burnham administration.

title: Ukraine thankful that intelligence on missile strikes ‘works now’, says Zelenskyy – as it happened
content_c:
Ukraine is thankful that intelligence on missile strikes 'works now,' Zelenskyy says
Zelenskyy says the talks covered security guarantees, among others, and he hopes to hear Russia’s response tomorrow.
He says Ukraine needs “strong security guarantees after the war ends.”
He also pointedly says that he is thankful that intelligence sharing “works now” (that’s my emphasis), and it helps with responding to any Russian attacks against Ukraine.
US envoy Witkoff to travel to Russia with new ideas discussed with Ukraine, Europe - summary
Jakub Krupa
US peace envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to St Petersburg on Wednesday to relay to Russia some new peace proposals discussed with Ukraine, Norway’s prime minister Jonas Gahr Støre said after hosting the US-Ukraine talks in Oslo (19:06).
The leaders discussed a number of contentious issues, including possible ceasefires, energy, and security guarantees (19:13).
Zelenskyy also confirmed that Ukraine is “now” again receiving US intelligence about Russia’s strikes (19:22), after his earlier discussions with US secretary of state Marco Rubio (19:10, 19:16).
Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy suggestedthat any final peace deal would require a trilateral summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, as some outstanding issues are of such gravity that “only the leaders” can resolve them (19:10).
Zelenskyy stressed that “Ukraine wants peace more than anyone,” but insisted “nothing [gets discussed] about Ukraine without Ukraine.”
Finland’s influential president Alexander Stubb said today’s talks put the peace process “back on track” with good progress “on a technical level,” as he hoped for a good outcome from Witkoff’s discussions with Russia on Wednesday (19:13, 19:28).
A further summary of earlier events today is here.
Peace process 'back on track,' hopeful Stubb says ahead of Witkoff's talks with Russia
In his closing comments, Finland’s Stubb says “it was a good day for peace,” as he acknowledges that “the top priority of the US administration is to find a peaceful solution to Russia’s war of aggression in Ukraine.”
He repeats that they “have made a lot of progress under the radar in the past week or so.”
“I feel that the process is back on track, and we’ll continue to work on it together with our European friends.
The key, of course, will be, what kind of messages Steve Witkoff will be able to get from St Petersburg tomorrow. But I think today was a success, and tomorrow is a new day. Hopefully we don’t do any backtrack[ing].”
'Nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine,' Zelenskyy insists
Zelenskyy gets asked if today’s meeting changes his view that the US is trying to pressure Ukraine to capitulate, and reports of a possible US, China, Russia trilateral meeting.
He stresses the principle of “nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine.”
“So I don’t know what about the trilateral meeting will be between America, China and, Russia? It’s up to them. But of course, if this is about Ukraine, our future, it can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations.”
He says the talks between Ukraine, Europe and the US have been constructive, “and we will see what will be tomorrow” in St. Petersburg.
Norway’s Støre repeats his positive lines on today’s talks which he says allowed both sides to “straighten out a few things and to agree that what matters now is to look ahead.”
He pointedly thanks Witkoff and hopes for a good outcome from his talks with Russia tomorrow (which he curiously says will be in Moscow, not St Petersburg, as said earlier).
“We are on a certain track, but war is unpredictable. It doesn’t follow a plan. And that’s why from time to time, we have to use, some cool diplomatic political brains to get our thinking back on track and our planning back on track.”
Ukraine is thankful that intelligence on missile strikes 'works now,' Zelenskyy says
Zelenskyy says the talks covered security guarantees, among others, and he hopes to hear Russia’s response tomorrow.
He says Ukraine needs “strong security guarantees after the war ends.”
He also pointedly says that he is thankful that intelligence sharing “works now” (that’s my emphasis), and it helps with responding to any Russian attacks against Ukraine.
Norway’s Støre jumps in to respond to a question on why Witkoff is not answering questions with the three other leaders.
He diplomatically points out that “this is a press conference among political leaders,” hinting that Witkoff is essentially of a different diplomatic rank.
But more broadly, he talks about the process, and the need for Europe “to be at the table.”
“To succeed, to achieve a last and fair piece, we need an equation of us, Ukraine, Russia and Europe and basically also other key countries, because this is a war with huge ramifications.”
He says he and Stubb don’t talk “on behalf of Europe,” but both countries, neighbours of Russia, have a deep understanding of the challenges faced by Europe.
Finland’s Stubb jumps in to add that they just work “in the back office” of the talks to support their progress.
He says Norway and Finland take part “because we believe in international law, but also based on self-interest” as Russia’s neighbours with “our history with Russia.”
“We’ll see what happens after tomorrow in Saint Petersburg. It’s very important that the American negotiators and President Trump stay engaged.”
Zelenskyy hints at further talks with US Rubio in the next 48 hours
Asked about his confidence in doing deal with Trump, Zelenskyy is very diplomatic.
He goes back to his conversation with Rubio earlier today, and says it was the right channel to discuss “sensitive issues” such as Stalink, interceptors, and intelligence sharing.
He says he hopes to talk with Rubio again in the next 48 hours.
In the Q&A, Ukraine’s Zelenskyy gets asked about his concessions and whether he is losing the war now.
He says the discussions revolved around “sensitive” issues, but he wants to “push as quick as possible to end this war” and focus next discussions on reconstruction.
He insists “we are not losing the war,” but concedes that “we are losing people and time,” as “our children do not have real life, childhood.”
He says “that is why we need to end this war as quick as possible.”
'Peace requires patience, but unfortunately war does not wait,' Stubb says as he hails 'genuine progress'
Finland’s Stubb says he believes today’s talks achieved some “genuine” progress “on two levels: … the short term and the big picture.”
“We found some elements of peace which will be taken forward to Saint Petersburg tomorrow.”
He says the discussions focused on “key issues such as air defence, energy installations, and partial ceasefires, such as those on energy and food security,” building on discussions in Miami.
Stubb says he understand “there has been a lot of noise” but “on a technical level, I feel that we are on the same page, and the next steps are about how we get there.”
“In my experience, peace requires patience, but unfortunately war does not wait. People are dying every day and each day. Our job is to do what we can to end it. And I think today was a step in the right direction.”
'Ukraine wants peace more than anyone,' Zelenskyy says as he calls for trilateral meeting with US, Russia
Ukraine’s Zelenskyy is up next.
He thanks Norway for hosting the talks, and Finland’s Stubb for joining the process.
He says today’s talk with the US were “important” as he says all parties need to “keep talking at all levels and work together on the decisions needed to end this war.”
He thanks US secretary of state Marco Rubio for their earlier phone call conversation, too.
He says:
“Ukraine wants peace more than anyone. It was Russia who started this war, and the decision to keep the killing going is Russia’s choice and Russia’s alone.”
He adds:
“We are working to find a solution. I thought we have some clear ideas on how to get to peace, and we are united with our European partners in this effort, and we want the Americans to take these ideas to the Russians.”
He says he wants a trilateral meeting of the leaders – that’s Trump, Putin and himself – because there are issues that “only the leaders” can resolve.
Norway’s Støre hails 'positive' meeting with Witkoff flying to Russia to discuss proposals tomorrow
Norway’s Støre is the first to speak.
He says Norway remains supportive of Ukraine, and “we have always made it clear there will be nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine.”
He thanks Trump’s envoys Witkoff and Kushner for joining the talks, and says:
“We believe that peace is possible and necessary for Ukraine and for Europe and for the entire world. We have hosted today, I would say, good and constructive talks, necessary after events of the last week. We have agreed that working together is crucial.”
He says US’s Witkoff will fly to St. Petersburg tomorrow to relay the result of today’s proposals to Russia, and “possibly pave the way for a meeting at the leaders’ level.”
“We have discussed today issues linked to security for Ukraine, prosperity plan after the war; issues related to territory and issues related to sanctions and questions related to European security order in the aftermath of this war.”
We are waiting for press conference after Ukraine-US talks in Oslo
Jakub Krupa
We are now pausing our coverageas we wait for the Ukraine-US talks in Oslo to wrap up.
I will be back when the leaders of Ukraine, Norway and Finland show up for their press conference, which is currently expected around 6pm UK (7pm Oslo). We will bring you the presser live here.
In the meantime, here’s the summary of the day so far:
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy is in Oslo, holding talks with the US peace envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, with the Norwegian PM Støre and Finnish president Stubb also attending (12:23, 13:22, 16:06).
French authorities said that military forces will be deployed to reinforce “massive” police presence during the upcoming protests on Saturday (15:29, 15:57), as they framed the worsening situation as a choice between “violence and the Republic.”
Italian defence minister Guido Crosetto warned that city riots, seen also in the Italian city of Milan, are part of a broader “hybrid war” against the west, with younger people radicalising through the use of social media platforms (15:21), with the Italian government planning to approve new security measures (14:27).
In other news,
EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the bloc’s relationship with the UK is of “vital importance in the current geopolitical, security and economic context,” as he set out the bloc’s expectations ahead of next month’s EU-UK summit on 20 November (11:44).
UN human rights chief condemns protests violence, worries about 'excessive use of force' by authorities
Meanwhile, UN Human Rights chief Volker Türk has condemned “all acts of violence” during the last week’s protests in Albania, Belgium, France, Italy and Portugal, and called on all parties to “reduce tensions and prevent further violence.”
In a statement he insisted that “the best and only way forward is inclusive and safe dialogue.”
Türk continued:
“People have the right to protest peacefully, and to have their voices heard. States must facilitate these rights.
I deplore the actions of those exploiting protests to commit acts of violence and vandalism against public and private property. They should be held individually accountable.
I am concerned by reports of unnecessary and excessive use of force against protesters, including children. States must ensure that any law enforcement response remains lawful, necessary and proportionate. Allegations of unlawful use of force must be investigated promptly, effectively and independently, with accountability and effective remedies for victims.
I note some steps already taken by authorities to investigate incidents and ease tensions. I further urge States to engage protesters, particularly young people, in meaningful, inclusive and constructive dialogue, and to take concrete steps to address legitimate and fundamental human rights concerns over education, public services, housing, the rising cost of living and inequality.”
A short press release issued by the police quoted the head of investigation at the North Jutland force saying that “this is a case we are taking very seriously.”
The case focuses on suspected cooperation with foreign intelligence and has been brought forward in partnership with the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, the police said, without disclosing more detail.
The two men – which DR says are aged 18 and 21 – were arrested yesterday, and a preliminary court hearing is now getting under way.
But DR notes that the case is unusual given the hearing is taking place outside of regular court hours.
The incident comes less than a month after the Danish defence intelligence service issued a report warning against Russia’s activities.
For what it’s worth, we are expecting to hear from Zelenskyy, Stubb and Støre after today’s talks, probably around 6pm UK time (7pm Oslo).
We will bring you the key lines here, alongside a live stream to follow along.
In the last few minutes, Zelenskyy posted a video from today’s talks alongside the Norwegian and Finnish leaders, saying:
“Jonas, Alex, thank you for your unwavering support and DAILY attention to protecting lives. We are stronger together. Thank you, Norway! Thank you, Finland!”

title: Who are the women powering India's youth-led 'Cockroach' protests?
content_c:
Who are the women powering India's youth-led 'Cockroach' protests?
October 20, 2026
On July 20, Navkiran Natt and her partner set out for the magistrate's office in New Delhi to get married. They arrived to find a tense situation, with police gathering to break up a youth-led march on Parliament. Office staff — and the couple's wedding witnesses — were running late due to barricades.
The protest movement known as the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) had announced the march to demand the resignation of India's then-Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The protesters were met with heavy resistance from security forces, who had deployed batons, tear gas and pellet-firing shotguns, leading to injuries and mass detentions.
Less than three months later, on October 10, Natt left home early in the morning and spent the day crisscrossing the locked-down Indian capital looking for a protest she could join.
"The success of this protest is not how many people will reach Jantar Mantar," she told DW, referring to the protest site in central New Delhi. "It's that even after all this barricading and state violence, people are leaving their homes to join."
What are these protests about?
The CJP began as a satirical online movement after the chief justice of India, Surya Kant, referred to unemployed young people as "cockroaches" in an offhand remark. The name is an ironic riff on the name of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
After succeeding in seeing Pradhan step down in late July, the CJP is now demanding the resignation of the country's controversy-hit Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after more than 130 million names were removed from draft electoral rolls nationwide.
With CJP leadership in judicial custody or under threat of detention, one name has fast become synonymous with the demonstrations: student leader Neha Bora, who prefers to use the pronoun they/them.
Bora has run through the streets to dodge police officials, climbed barricades in the face of security personnel, shouted slogans from detention vans and addressed press conferences alongside CJP spokespersons and others.
They are the president of the All India Students' Association, the student wing of the Communist Party of India (Marxist–Leninist) Liberation (CPI-ML).
"In extremely disappointing, fearful, tyrannical times, people try to gather hope from whatever source they can … If these people are fighting, then probably we can also fight," Bora told DW.
"It is a responsibility that you owe to people," they added.
Women out on the streets in large numbers
The Cockroach-led demonstrations also come at a time when women and members of the LGBTQ+ community are calling for greater autonomy for women in the aftermath of the gang rape of a 17-year-old girl in New Delhi in late September, placing the issue of safety in India back into the spotlight.
According to the National Crime Records Bureau, 441,534 cases of crimes against women were registered in 2024, averaging 1,210 cases per day. Experts say these official statistics can only give a partial account of gendered violence.
But despite facing sexualized backlash from police on the streets and from online mobs, the women and genderqueer people leading the movement reject being cast as victims.
"The "beti bachao" [save the daughter] thing just doesn't cut it with this generation. It is a very specific ask: see us as political beings, free beings," activist Kavita Krishnan told DW.
"Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao" (Save the Daughter, Educate the Daughter) is a flagship BJP government program launched in 2015.
Protest as daily life
These days, Gurmehar Kaur's day starts like any other — a workout or a yoga class — and often ends with Indian Youth Congress' lawyers getting her released from police detention.
"Resistance can't be a separate event … a big day, and then you go back to your regular life," she told DW.
The 29-year-old author of "The Young and the Restless: Youth and Politics in India" spent a better part of the last decade in the public eye.
This year, she joined the youth wing of India's main opposition party, The Congress, whose offices are located a stone's throw away from Jantar Mantar, the hub of the last wave of protests.
Kaur said her political association has given her access to resources that can support the movement, offering a safety net for protesters "regardless of their political affiliation."
At a time when authorities are cracking down on CJP protesters, she said opposition members like her have a duty to fulfill: "Show up, put your body on the line."
Price of visibility
But showing up often comes with a cost, especially for women and queer protesters.
Kaur explained how male colleagues often "feel quite elated when their photos are in the media." However, for her, "attention is equal to death and rape threats and humiliation and abuse."
Navkiran Natt, an activist most significantly associated with the 2020–2021 farmers' protests, echoes Kaur's experience.
"If a woman is leading the protest, the first attack is on her sexuality," she said.
Social media images have shown women protesters with their clothes torn during clashes with police.
Delhi officials have denied allegations of manhandling, adding that women protesters were treated with "dignity."
Student leader Bora refuted the police's claim, saying that a small number of female personnel were available to handle a large number of female protesters.
"Several women protesters came to protect me and prevent me from getting detained," they said.
Authorities have registered a police case against a journalist who accused a senior Delhi police officer of sexual harassment under an Indian law meant to prevent crimes against members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. They say her own allegations are under investigation.
The internet was also flooded with AI-made, sexualized images of women protesters edited into protest photos.
Why activists say the tactic is failing
This has not prevented protesters from taking to the streets even the day after being detained by authorities.
"They don't know what they're dealing with," activist Krishnan said, referring to the government's crackdown on demonstrators.
She said authorities assume sexual humiliation will scare women off, but "this is not a generation that thinks of… sexual violence as being something shameful."
She was at the forefront of demonstrations after the 2012 "Nirbhaya" gang rape, where slogans like "Hang the rapists" were seen in public. This time, however, she said the anger "is not going to be about masculine displays of honor."
It is about "dignity and freedom ... Women face all kinds of problems in every country, and Indian women are no different," she added.
Krishnan said the youth-led protests are part of a wider global wave of "civilizational, cultural nationalism," which uses gender and the language of protection, whether of daughters, families or tradition, to rally support against minorities, immigrants and trans people.
"You listen to the rhetoric of Donald Trump or Viktor Orban or the Alternative for Germany (AfD). It is the same," she said, referring to politics in the United States and Europe. "If you look at what's happening in India, you may be able to better understand what's happening in your country."
These young Indians, she said, are refusing to be taken in. They are "fighting back for a language of the future, a language that has hope."

Who are the women powering India's youth-led 'Cockroach' protests?

On July 20, Navkiran Natt and her partner set out for the magistrate's office in New Delhi to get married. They arrived to find a tense situation, with police gathering to break up a youth-led march on Parliament. Office staff — and the couple's wedding witnesses — were running late due to barricades.
The protest movement known as the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) had announced the march to demand the resignation of India's then-Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The protesters were met with heavy resistance from security forces, who had deployed batons, tear gas and pellet-firing shotguns, leading to injuries and mass detentions.
Less than three months later, on October 10, Natt left home early in the morning and spent the day crisscrossing the locked-down Indian capital looking for a protest she could join.
"The success of this protest is not how many people will reach Jantar Mantar," she told DW, referring to the protest site in central New Delhi. "It's that even after all this barricading and state violence, people are leaving their homes to join."

The CJP began as a satirical online movement after the chief justice of India, Surya Kant, referred to unemployed young people as "cockroaches" in an offhand remark. The name is an ironic riff on the name of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
After succeeding in seeing Pradhan step down in late July, the CJP is now demanding the resignation of the country's controversy-hit Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after more than 130 million names were removed from draft electoral rolls nationwide.

Bora has run through the streets to dodge police officials, climbed barricades in the face of security personnel, shouted slogans from detention vans and addressed press conferences alongside CJP spokespersons and others.
They are the president of the All India Students' Association, the student wing of the Communist Party of India (Marxist–Leninist) Liberation (CPI-ML).

title: Prinz Harry: Streit mit Vater und Bruder soll beigelegt werden
content_c:
Zoff der britischen Royals Prinz Harry will sich mit Vater und Bruder vertragen
Prinz Harry, 42, will einen Schlussstrich unter den Streit mit dem Königshaus ziehen und den Zwist mit seinem Vater und Bruder beenden. Das sagte er in einem Interview mit dem »GQ«-Magazin.
»Es wurden einige Schlachten geschlagen, und das war auch notwendig«, so Harry. Die Spannungen in der britischen königlichen Familie seien etwas, das viele Menschen fasziniere, weil sie es auf sich selbst und ihre eigenen Familien übertragen könnten. »Es gibt Konflikte zwischen Geschwistern. Es gibt kaputte Beziehungen zwischen Kindern und ihren Eltern. Das begegnet mir die ganze Zeit, wenn ich mit Menschen spreche«, sagte er dem Magazin.
Der jüngere Sohn von König Charles III., 77, glaubt, dass sich andere bei ihm möglicherweise auch Hinweise erhoffen, wie sie ihre eigenen familiären Probleme lösen können. »Ich will eine Lösung finden«, betonte Harry. Mit all dem, was in der Welt vor sich gehe, sei es das Wichtigste, sich zu versöhnen.
Harry und seine Frau Meghan Markle, 45, hatten sich Anfang 2020 im Streit aus dem engeren Kreis der Königsfamilie losgesagt und zogen für mehrere Jahre in den US-Bundesstaat Kalifornien.
Seitdem hat sich der Graben weiter vertieft. In einem Interview mit der Talkshow-Legende Oprah Winfrey und einer Netflix-Doku packten die beiden aus. Spätestens seit Harry in seiner Autobiografie »Spare« (»Reserve«) mit William und anderen Royals abrechnete, ist das Tischtuch zerschnitten. Insbesondere das Verhältnis zu seinem Bruder, Prinz William, 44, soll zerrüttet sein.
Erst im Spätsommer dieses Jahres kehrten der Herzog und die Herzog von Sussex, wie das Paar auch genannt wird, mit ihren Kindern wieder nach Großbritannien zurück. Charles III. hatte Anfang September klargestellt, dass Harry und dessen Frau ungeachtet der Rückkehr nach Großbritannien weiterhin keine »arbeitenden Mitglieder« der Königsfamilie sind. In einem offiziellen Schreiben erklärte er, dass die Stellung des Paares »der von Privatpersonen gleicht« und die beiden nicht mit »Seine/Ihre Königliche Hoheit« angesprochen werden.

title: Flugausfälle: EU regelt Erstattung bei Buchung über Drittanbieter
content_c:
Bei Flugausfällen EU regelt Erstattung bei Buchung über Drittanbieter
In Zukunft müssen auch Drittanbieter die Kosten für die Buchung eines Fluges erstatten, wenn dieser ausfällt. Das hat das EU-Parlament beschlossen. Außerdem soll es ein einheitliches Erstattungsformular für so gut wie alle Transportmittel geben.
Wer einen Flug über einen Drittanbieter gebucht hat, soll bei Ausfällen künftig ebenso sein Geld zurück bekommen wie bei einer Buchung direkt bei der Fluggesellschaft.
Das Europaparlament stimmte in Straßburg für ein Gesetz, das die Drittanbieter - also zum Beispiel Online-Reiseplattformen - zur Erstattung verpflichtet. Auch angefallene Vermittlungsgebühren müssen demnach zurückgezahlt werden.
Ein einheitliches Formular
Auf der Internetseite der EU-Kommission soll es in Zukunft außerdem ein allgemeines Formular zum Herunterladen geben, mit dem Passagiere eine Erstattung oder Entschädigung beantragen können - egal ob beim Transport mit Flug, Bus, Bahn oder Fähre.
"Wir schaffen etwas Neues für alle Verkehrsträger", sagt der CDU-Europaabgeordnete Jens Giesecke: "Wir sorgen dafür, dass die Rechte einfacher duchsetzbar sind. Wir haben keinen Bürokratie-Dschungel mehr, sondern nur noch ein einziges Formular. Das ist ein großer Fortschritt und macht alles einfacher."
Auch die Barrierefreiheit soll spürbar verbessert werden. Im Flugzeug dürfen Begleitpersonen für Menschen mit Behinderungen künftig kostenlos mitfliegen. Für Bus und Bahn gibt es diese Regel schon. Außerdem soll EU-weit einheitlich definiert werden, welche Hunde als Assistenzhunde zugelassen werden.
Ein Jahr Zeit für Umsetzung
Die Transportunternehmen und Buchungsportale haben ein Jahr Zeit, um sich umzustellen. Die nationalen Aufsichtsbehörden - etwa das Luftfahrt-Bundesamt in Deutschland - sollen dann prüfen, dass die Branche sich an die neuen Regeln hält. Verstoßen Unternehmen gegen das Recht, müssen sie mit Bußgeldern rechnen.
Die neuen Regeln sind eine Ergänzung für die Fluggastrechtereform, die im Sommer beschlossen wurde. In dem Regelwerk ging es unter anderem um mehr Übersichtlichkeit bei den Zusatzkosten für das Gepäck.
Die EU setzt mit den Regeln eine Reihe von Urteilen des Europäischen Gerichtshofs (EuGH) in geltendes Recht um. Der Rat der 27 EU-Länder muss den Änderungen noch final zustimmen, das gilt aber als Formalie. Damit wird ein erbittert geführter politischer Kampf zu Ende gehen. Verbraucherschützer sprechen vom härtesten Tauziehen für Verbraucherrechte überhaupt in der Geschichte der EU.
Mit Informationen von Andreas Meyer-Feist, ARD Brüssel

title: Россия распродает золотые резервы рекордными с 1998 года темпами
content_c:
Центробанк России десятый месяц подряд распродает золото из своих резервов в рамках операций по покрытию дефицита бюджета, который в этом году вдвое превысит первоначальные планы и достигнет 7,3 трлн рублей, пишет The Moscow Times.
Как сообщил во вторник Банк России, в сентябре золотой запас РФ сократился ещё на 0,2 млн тройских унций (около 6,2 тонны), а его общий объем снизился до 72,8 млн унций — самого низкого уровня с конца 2019 года.
С декабря, когда российский Центробанк начал крупнейшую за несколько десятилетий распродажу золота, его запасы сократились на 2 млн тройских унций, или примерно 62 тонны.
Согласно статистике Международного валютного фонда, лишь однажды в современной истории Россия распродавала золотые резервы быстрее.
В 1998 году, на фоне дефолта, валютного кризиса и краха пирамиды государственных краткосрочных облигаций (ГКО), Центробанк за три месяца продал 3,8 млн тройских унций золота (118 тонн).
Правда, к концу года часть слитков выкупили обратно, поэтому по итогам 1998 года золотой запас Центробанка сократился на 1,6 млн унций (около 50 тонн). Это даже меньше, чем Россия продала в этом году.
В дальнейшем Кремль преимущественно накапливал золото в резервах. С конца 1990-х годов золотой запас России вырос более чем в пять раз. На начало 2022 года он составлял 74 млн тройских унций, или около 2,3 тысячи тонн, и занимал пятое место в мире по объему.
Почему Россия вынуждена продавать золотые резервы
Распродажа, начавшаяся в конце прошлого года, сделала российский Центробанк крупнейшим продавцом золота среди центральных банков мира.
Эти операции связаны с так называемым зеркалированием операций Министерства финансов РФ с активами Фонда национального благосостояния (ФНБ). Центробанк продает на рынке золото ФНБ, которое ранее Минфин уже реализовал в рамках операций по покрытию бюджетного дефицита.
«Минфин использует накопленные резервы (в частности, в золоте) для покрытия бюджетного дефицита при недостатке доходов. Поскольку в 2026 году нефтегазовые доходы сократились, это привело к увеличению продаж активов Фонда национального благосостояния (ФНБ), в том числе и золота», — объясняет аналитик «Финама» Александр Потавин.
Кроме того, за счёт продажи золота Центробанк может компенсировать недостаток валютной ликвидности.
По мнению Потавина, высокие мировые цены на золото, вероятно, также способствовали принятию решения об активизации продажи драгоценного металла.
Китай скупает российское золото в рекордных объемах
Часть проданного российского золота попадает в Китай, который в этом году увеличил закупки драгоценного металла в России до исторических максимумов.
По данным китайской таможни, в январе–июле в Гонконг поступило около 100 тонн золота российского происхождения. Это в три раза больше, чем за аналогичный период прошлого года.
После того как лондонский рынок — крупнейший в мире — закрылся для российского золота, поставщики из РФ начали переориентировать экспорт на восток, отмечает аналитик LSEG Дебаджит Саха.
Потоки российского золота в Китай резко выросли уже в первый год полномасштабной войны против Украины. По подсчётам Financial Times, с тех пор через Гонконг было экспортировано российского драгоценного металла на 35 млрд долларов.
description: Все, чтобы залатать дыру в бюджете.
content:
Центробанк России десятый месяц подряд распродает золото из своих резервов в рамках операций по покрытию дефицита бюджета, который в этом году вдвое превысит первоначальные планы и достигнет 7,3 трлн рублей, пишет The Moscow Times.
Как сообщил во вторник Банк России, в сентябре золотой запас РФ сократился ещё на 0,2 млн тройских унций (около 6,2 тонны), а его общий объем снизился до 72,8 млн унций — самого низкого уровня с конца 2019 года.
С декабря, когда российский Центробанк начал крупнейшую за несколько десятилетий распродажу золота, его запасы сократились на 2 млн тройских унций, или примерно 62 тонны.
Согласно статистике Международного валютного фонда, лишь однажды в современной истории Россия распродавала золотые резервы быстрее.

title: "Метінвест" зміцнив свої гарантовані обов'язки перед партнерами за рахунок ще одної своєї компанії
content_c:
Metinvest B.V. (Нідерланди), материнська компанія міжнародної вертикально інтегрованої гірничо-металургійної групи компаній, зміцнила свої гарантовані обов'язки перед партнерами за рахунок ще однієї своєї структури.
"Metinvest B.V., беручи до уваги чинні обмеження, встановлені законодавством України щодо транскордонних платежів в іноземній валюті за межі України, цим повідомляє про призначення ТОВ "Індастріал Коул Холдінг" (новий гарант) додатковим гарантом стосовно кожного випуску облігацій", – констатується у інформації компанії на біржі 20 єовтня.
При цьому уточнюється, що "Новий гарант уклав договори поруки стосовно кожного випуску облігацій, відповідно до яких він, разом з іншими гарантами (на умовах солідарної відповідальності), гарантує виконання грошових зобов'язань емітента, що виникають згідно з договором довірчого управління (Trust Deed), облігаціями та Агентською угодою, відповідно до умов (Conditions). Терміни, вжиті у цьому повідомленні з великої літери, якщо вони не визначені в цьому повідомленні, мають значення, надані їм в умовах", – пояснюється в повідомленні.
"Метінвест" є вертикально інтегрованою групою з видобувних і металургійних підприємств. Його підприємства розташовані в Україні – в Донецькій, Луганській, Запорізькій і Дніпропетровській областях, а також у країнах Європи. Основними акціонерами холдингу є група "СКМ" (71,24%) і "Смарт-холдинг" (23,76%). ТОВ "Метінвест Холдинг" – керуюча компанія групи "Метінвест".

title: 'Trash Island' or DC landmark? How a golf course got Trump in a messy legal dispute
content_c:
'Trash Island' or DC landmark? How a golf course got Trump in a messy legal dispute
- Published
For Jourdain Yardan, golfing at the East Potomac Golf Links on Washington DC's waterfront is a twice-weekly ritual.
"Anyone from any walk of life, whether they're starting to play golf or whether they're a ... seasoned golfer, they can come out here and play golf at a pretty reasonable rate," the 35-year-old told the BBC while putting on the course on Monday.
But President Donald Trump does not seem convinced of its charms, calling the 106-year-old course "Trash Island" Monday evening on Truth Social.
Now, he intends to shut it down for renovations to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments".
The renovation is part of the president's sprawling and controversial efforts to shape the US capital, which include a new White House ballroom, a 250-foot-tall arch and other changes to longstanding landmarks. The golf course is a smaller project, but deeply personal to many who live in the city.
Yardan described a potential shuttering, even if temporary, as a "huge dent" in DC culture that could change the heart of the space.
Trump, an avid golfer and owner of more than a dozen courses, says his vision for the course will make it "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World".
But courts will need to mediate the dispute between the White House and the community before Trump can realize his plans.
The historic course, which sits 2 miles (3km) south of the White House, is one of three public courses run by the National Park Service in the nation's capital. A lawsuit from the DC Preservation League and two golfers from the course asks the court to stop Trump's planned renovation.
"Our litigation is intended to protect this community jewel for the people and communities it serves," Democracy Forward, the group representing the plaintiffs, said in a statement on social media.
The legal fight intensified this month after the government began large-scale tree removal on the course without giving the court or plaintiffs notice.
A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to stop its redevelopment plans until at least 26 October.
Despite the work stoppage, Trump took to social media on Sunday to announce that the course will be closed for 15-months beginning in November to accommodate the renovations. He also shared a rendering of the course redesign.
"The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous, and disease-infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall," Trump wrote in his post on Sunday.
While golfer Thomas Snow, who is not part of the suit, conceded the course could use a "facelift", he thinks the president's description of the course is a "gross overstatement".
Currently, East Potomac does not offer the manicured experience one might find at the luxury, private golf courses the president is known for building. The public course is open to all and does not require a membership to access.
The facilities at the DC course are more modest, offering food court-style dining rather than amenities such as white tablecloth restaurants and upscale locker rooms.
Golfers like Snow and Yardan who regularly play the courses at East Potomac, told the BBC it offers a rare combination of affordability and proximity to the city.
"You start to clear everything out and it just starts to become an empty plot of land that you just hit golf balls on; I think it gets rid of the culture of the golf course," Yardan said.
As a 70-year-old golfer, Snow pays $29 (£21.65) for 18 holes when he visits East Potomac.
"There's no place in the whole DMV (the metropolitan region including DC and its Maryland and Virginia suburbs) that you can play a nice 18 holes for that price point," he said.
Snow worries that if Trump's proposal moves forward, people will be priced out.
Yardan, the twice-weekly golfer, echoed those concerns.
"Anytime you hear about big league, big golfers, that also includes big prices," he said. "The biggest thing that I like about this golf course .. is that it's affordable," he said.
description: Trump said he has plans to turn a 106-year-old public golf course in Washington DC into a tournament-capable golf course for pros, but local golfers are not happy.

title: Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats
content_c:
Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats
- Published
UK net migration has dropped to the lowest level, outside of the Covid pandemic, since 2012.
How does that sit alongside other key migration measures, including asylum applications, small boat arrivals and visas granted?
Scroll down to find out more about the latest key figures, and get answers to key questions on a range of topics.
- Is the government meeting its pledges on illegal immigration and asylum? 
  - Published26 February
- Why do Channel migrants want to come to the UK? 
  - Published9 July 2025
- Find out more about people crossing the Channel in small boats 
  - Published22 October 2025
Produced by: Rob England, Libby Rogers, Jess Carr, Aidan McNamee, John Walton, Becky Dale, Allison Shultes, Chris Kay, Steven Connor and Scott Jarvis.
Graphics by: Jez Frazer, Zoe Bartholomew and Joy Roxas
About the data
Figures from government and other official sources can be revised between publications. This page shows data as presented in the latest available release.
Immigration, emigration and net migration
*The net migration figure for the UK will not exactly equal immigration minus emigration because the Office for National Statistics (ONS) publishes it as a rounded number.
Immigration and emigration estimates, external from the ONS are updated twice a year.
Net migration figures use the internationally recognised definition of a long-term migrant: "A person who moves to a country other than that of their usual residence for at least a year."
Visas for legal migration
The total number of visa entries only includes visas that have been granted. It does not include visitor visas or transit visas, where the UK is not the final destination.
Visa figures record when permission was granted, not when or whether someone arrived in the UK.
If a person was granted more than one visa within the year shown, each visa is counted separately.
Work visas refer to new individuals granted permission, or extensions of existing permission. This includes categories such as seasonal work, health and care, domestic worker and youth mobility visas.
Study visas include all individuals sponsored by approved UK education providers, as well as those on short-term study visas.
Family visas allow someone to come to or remain in the UK to live with close family members already here. This includes joining a spouse, partner, child or parent, or coming to care for a relative.
The "Other" category includes visas outside work, study and family routes. This covers humanitarian schemes such as the Ukraine Sponsorship Scheme and the British National (Overseas) route. It also includes family permits for people from European Union or European Economic Area countries.
Asylum applications and accommodation
Home Office figures for asylum seekers in hotels are published under the category "contingency accommodation - hotel".
The number of people in all other forms of accommodation includes non-hotel contingency accommodation, as well as initial, dispersal and "other" accommodation.
To show how evenly accommodation is distributed, a scale compares each local authority's share of people in that type of accommodation with the UK-wide average for areas using the same accommodation type:
- Less than half – more than 50% below the average share
- Lower than – between 25% and 50% below the average share
- About the same as – within 25% of the average share
- Higher than – between 25% and 100% above the average share
- More than double – more than 100% above the average share
Backlog figures for people waiting for an initial asylum decision include both main applicants and dependants.
Open appeals against refused asylum applications refer to individuals. Figures on appeals are published every three months by the Ministry of Justice, at a different time from other government asylum statistics. It also includes a small number of appeals against revocation of protection.
Small boat crossings and other irregular arrivals
Small boat crossing figures and the average number of people per boat are taken from the Home Office daily data, external.
Entering the UK without permission is an offence under immigration law, external, but asylum seekers are generally not prosecuted if they claim asylum on arrival. In some cases, people have been prosecuted alongside other offences, such as people smuggling or re-entering after deportation.
The International Organization for Migration (IOM) collects figures on people who have died, external or gone missing while crossing from mainland Europe to the UK. These reports are based on information from French and UK officials (such as police or coastguard) and media sources. The IOM considers them an undercount because there are no official statistics.
The figures may include people who died in the Channel itself, as well as those who died while travelling to a crossing point.
Data on modern slavery includes final decisions only. Modern slavery covers human trafficking, slavery, servitude and forced labour.
Figures for other entries without permission combine all recorded irregular arrivals that were not by small boat. This includes inadequately documented air arrivals, recorded detections at UK ports, and other recorded detections within the UK.
Returns and deportations
People who are denied entry at the border and then leave the UK are not included in the returns figures on this page.
Returns involving the government are grouped into three categories. Enforced returns (which include deportations) are cases where the Home Office requires someone to leave and arranges their removal, usually because they have no legal right to remain or following a criminal conviction.
Assisted voluntary returns are when someone agrees to leave the UK and receives government support, such as help with travel documents, flights or reintegration assistance.
Controlled voluntary returns are when someone leaves the UK voluntarily without being forcibly removed, but their departure is formally recorded by the Home Office.
Independent returns are referred to by the government as "other verified returns," and refer to individuals who have left the UK without
People returned after a criminal conviction include non-British citizens convicted in the UK of any criminal offence, or convicted abroad of a serious criminal offence.
UK migration compared with other countries
Sea arrival figures are taken from the UNHCR European sea arrivals dashboard and combined with UK Home Office small boat data.
Asylum application, immigration and emigration figures for European countries are the latest available data from Eurostat for: Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Czechia, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia, Bulgaria, Romania, Norway, Switzerland and Croatia.
UK population figures are from ONS, National Records of Scotland and the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency 2024 mid-year estimates. European population figures are from Eurostat as of 1 January 2024.
To ensure comparability with the UK, European countries with populations under one million are excluded from per-capita comparisons of net migration and asylum applications.
For net migration comparisons, only countries that include asylum seekers or refugees in their immigration figures are included.
These are: Austria, Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Slovenia, Spain and Switzerland.

description: Use our interactive tracker to explore the latest migration statistics for the UK
content:
Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats
- Published
UK net migration has dropped to the lowest level, outside of the Covid pandemic, since 2012.
How does that sit alongside other key migration measures, including asylum applications, small boat arrivals and visas granted?
Scroll down to find out more about the latest key figures, and get answers to key questions on a range of topics.
- Is the government meeting its pledges on illegal immigration and asylum? 
  - Published26 February
- Why do Channel migrants want to come to the UK? 
  - Published9 July 2025
- Find out more about people crossing the Channel in small boats 
  - Published22 October 2025
Produced by: Rob England, Libby Rogers, Jess Carr, Aidan McNamee, John Walton, Becky Dale, Allison Shultes, Chris Kay, Steven Connor and Scott Jarvis.
Graphics by: Jez Frazer, Zoe Bartholomew and Joy Roxas
About the data
Figures from government and other official sources can be revised between publications. This page shows data as presented in the latest available release.
Immigration, emigration and net migration
*The net migration figure for the UK will not exactly equal immigration minus emigration because the Office for National Statistics (ONS) publishes it as a rounded number.
Immigration and emigration estimates, external from the ONS are updated twice a year.
Net migration figures use the internationally recognised definition of a long-term migrant: "A person who moves to a country other than that of their usual residence for at least a year."
Visas for legal migration
The total number of visa entries only includes visas that have been granted. It does not include visitor visas or transit visas, where the UK is not the final destination.
Visa figures record when permission was granted, not when or whether someone arrived in the UK.
If a person was granted more than one visa within the year shown, each visa is counted separately.
Work visas refer to new individuals granted permission, or extensions of existing permission. This includes categories such as seasonal work, health and care, domestic worker and youth mobility visas.
Study visas include all individuals sponsored by approved UK education providers, as well as those on short-term study visas.
Family visas allow someone to come to or remain in the UK to live with close family members already here. This includes joining a spouse, partner, child or parent, or coming to care for a relative.
The "Other" category includes visas outside work, study and family routes. This covers humanitarian schemes such as the Ukraine Sponsorship Scheme and the British National (Overseas) route. It also includes family permits for people from European Union or European Economic Area countries.
Asylum applications and accommodation
Home Office figures for asylum seekers in hotels are published under the category "contingency accommodation - hotel".
The number of people in all other forms of accommodation includes non-hotel contingency accommodation, as well as initial, dispersal and "other" accommodation.
To show how evenly accommodation is distributed, a scale compares each local authority's share of people in that type of accommodation with the UK-wide average for areas using the same accommodation type:
- Less than half – more than 50% below the average share
- Lower than – between 25% and 50% below the average share
- About the same as – within 25% of the average share
- Higher than – between 25% and 100% above the average share
- More than double – more than 100% above the average share
Backlog figures for people waiting for an initial asylum decision include both main applicants and dependants.
Open appeals against refused asylum applications refer to individuals. Figures on appeals are published every three months by the Ministry of Justice, at a different time from other government asylum statistics. It also includes a small number of appeals against revocation of protection.
Small boat crossings and other irregular arrivals
Small boat crossing figures and the average number of people per boat are taken from the Home Office daily data, external.
Entering the UK without permission is an offence under immigration law, external, but asylum seekers are generally not prosecuted if they claim asylum on arrival. In some cases, people have been prosecuted alongside other offences, such as people smuggling or re-entering after deportation.
The International Organization for Migration (IOM) collects figures on people who have died, external or gone missing while crossing from mainland Europe to the UK. These reports are based on information from French and UK officials (such as police or coastguard) and media sources. The IOM considers them an undercount because there are no official statistics.
The figures may include people who died in the Channel itself, as well as those who died while travelling to a crossing point.
Data on modern slavery includes final decisions only. Modern slavery covers human trafficking, slavery, servitude and forced labour.
Figures for other entries without permission combine all recorded irregular arrivals that were not by small boat. This includes inadequately documented air arrivals, recorded detections at UK ports, and other recorded detections within the UK.
Returns and deportations
People who are denied entry at the border and then leave the UK are not included in the returns figures on this page.
Returns involving the government are grouped into three categories. Enforced returns (which include deportations) are cases where the Home Office requires someone to leave and arranges their removal, usually because they have no legal right to remain or following a criminal conviction.
Assisted voluntary returns are when someone agrees to leave the UK and receives government support, such as help with travel documents, flights or reintegration assistance.
Controlled voluntary returns are when someone leaves the UK voluntarily without being forcibly removed, but their departure is formally recorded by the Home Office.
Independent returns are referred to by the government as "other verified returns," and refer to individuals who have left the UK without
People returned after a criminal conviction include non-British citizens convicted in the UK of any criminal offence, or convicted abroad of a serious criminal offence.
UK migration compared with other countries
Sea arrival figures are taken from the UNHCR European sea arrivals dashboard and combined with UK Home Office small boat data.
Asylum application, immigration and emigration figures for European countries are the latest available data from Eurostat for: Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Czechia, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia, Bulgaria, Romania, Norway, Switzerland and Croatia.
UK population figures are from ONS, National Records of Scotland and the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency 2024 mid-year estimates. European population figures are from Eurostat as of 1 January 2024.
To ensure comparability with the UK, European countries with populations under one million are excluded from per-capita comparisons of net migration and asylum applications.
For net migration comparisons, only countries that include asylum seekers or refugees in their immigration figures are included.
These are: Austria, Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Slovenia, Spain and Switzerland.
Portugal was also excluded as it did not have net migration data available for 2024, it will be re-included in future updates.

title: Troubled waters: life during wartime for Iranians on the strait of Hormuz
content_c:
Capt Farouq turns the wheel as he watches the ferry terminal of Bandar Abbas grow smaller, its bright lights flickering in the distance.
In front of him, the navigation radar beeps periodically, its green and pink lights glowing in the darkness. The ferry, today at about half capacity with roughly 100 passengers, turns and heads into the darkness of the strait of Hormuz.
Farouq, 39, sits comfortably in his cabin, overlooking the pitch black horizon as he sails towards Hormuz Island, a short commute of about half an hour from the Iranian mainland’s Haqqani Port, for 340,000 toman, about £1. He is relaxed and smiles as he pulls into the deeper waters. He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home.
Farouq says the crossings have not stopped since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on 28 February, although passenger numbers are down and the journey has become more dangerous. For months, Farouq has heard explosions coming from the strait, unclear as to whether that is air defence or attacks, or both. Tonight is no different.
Inside the ferry, passengers say they have gotten used to the sounds too, and, to an extent, the war itself. They drink tea and smoke cigarettes. Some nap, while others entertain their children. It’s hot and humid, the air thick, the windows fogged with condensation.
Even with a fragile ceasefire in place, here on the coast, it has barely felt as though the war has stopped.
According to Iranian government sources, attacks on the southern port of Bandar Abbas have damaged 760 fishing and commercial vessels. Farouq says his own ferry was also damaged by shrapnel while docked at the port, though it was quickly repaired.
Since the start of the war, Iranian forces have repeatedly attacked vessels attempting to cross the strait. In the first week of October alone, at least 12 attacks were reported against oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers, sending oil prices back above $100 a barrel.
With pressure mounting on the US president, Donald Trump, before the midterm elections, he is rumoured to be once again considering strikes.
But beyond the headlines and global markets, the strait is first and foremost a lifeline for many Iranians living in the southern province of Hormozgan.
Fishers, captains and harbour workers all depend on the strait for their livelihoods and the war has made their work increasingly difficult. Fishers can no longer venture as far out, ports have come under attack, and many people fled Bandar Abbas in the early months of the war for smaller, more remote villages in search of safety.
Anvar Sadat, a 38-year-old fisher who works at Bandar Abbas’s fish market, says business has slowed and that making ends meet has become increasingly difficult.
“Fishing boats can’t go out as freely as before the war, and our movement is restricted,” he says, adding that several of his colleagues in the city have been killed in attacks.
“This place was hell,” says Abdul Salam, a 45-year-old garbage collector. The beaches, particularly those near the port, were among the most dangerous places during the height of the war, he says, describing heavy attacks that forced him to stop working almost entirely to avoid the risk.
Life on the island, however, has been different, Farouq explains as he steers into the small, dimly lit port of Hormuz Island, his last crossing of the day before heading back to his family for the night.
Hormuz Island has long been known as a kind of “hippy paradise”, a place Iranians have come to regard as “free”. Artists and creatives moved here from bigger cities in search of peace; women swim in bathing suits, writers and painters find space to work, and life moves slower. There is “love and magic” here, as Yashar, a 35-year-old surfer, puts it, “a different rhythm”.
Life here has changed little, Yashar says, although the war has brought some new restrictions, and a handful of attacks, mostly on infrastructure. The roughly 8,000 residents are trying to support each other, and to preserve the sense of freedom that has set the island apart, he adds.
The government has closed off parts of Hormuz Island’s north, but beyond the now restricted areas, life has continued, he explains. “As long as you don’t go north, they leave you alone,” he says of the army.
“The tourism sector has taken the biggest hit,” says Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide, adding that he prefers to go by his first name only. “Guesthouses and homestays remain closed, as do restaurants and many cafes.” Visitors have largely stopped coming since the war, dealing a heavy blow to an island whose economy depends on tourism and fishing, both of which have been disrupted.
From the higher parts of the island, Omran says, it is possible to see deep into the strait on clear days, when the haze lifts and the humid air clears, all the way to the mountains of Khasab in Oman.
Residents have climbed up these barren mountains of red and white stone, at times watching the war unfold in the distance. Tankers remain stranded in the strait, explosions can be heard regularly. Yet residents also say the war has not driven them from the island.
Khaleh Kaniz, a 67-year-old painter who was born and raised on Hormuz, laughs when asked whether she had considered leaving in February, at the start of the war.
“Why should we leave? Where would we go? Our homes and our lives are here.”
